Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and the pleasure to present a petition that the Quebec National Assembly has already passed recognizing the importance of April 24 as the anniversary of the Armenian genocide.
The petitioners call upon Parliament to urge the government to offer its sympathy to the Armenian people, especially to Canadian Armenians who survived the genocide of April 24, 1915, and support the international lobbying efforts aimed at compelling the Tbrkish government to recognize and acknowledge the events of April 24, 1915.

Mr. Speaker, I have the privilege and honour to present a petition calling for the elimination of child poverty by the year 2000.
This petition is signed by a number of people in the province of Ontario, particularly in the city of Mississauga. It calls upon the government to make sure that its commitment of November 24, 1989 is complied with and that the government does everything in its power to work exclusively for the elimination of child poverty.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ELIMINATION OF VIOLENCE IN OUR SOCIETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table a petition from the Malartic School Board in Abitibi stating that films that portray violence on television are dangerous and should not be tolerated because they make violence seem desirable.

February 2, 1993
Routine Proceedings
The petition says that toys that are an incentive to violent games are unacceptable and their manufacture should be banned. The petition also points out that when acts of violence are reported, freedom of the press should be restricted, and that the repeated reporting of acts of violence on TV channels and on radio may lead to further, identical acts of violence.
Consequently your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to legislate a remedy to this problem in order to wipe out violence in our society and thus protect our children and provide all citizens with a better quality of life.

Mr. Speaker, this first petition is a request from citizens that the GST on books and other reading materials be removed. They point out that Canada has had a zero tax on these particular items since its beginning.
They also underline that reading, literacy and education are cornerstones of democracy and make a major contribution to the increase of productivity, effectiveness and efficiency in our nation.
They ask the government to review its policies and remove this tax.

Mr. Speaker, I have another petition. The petitioners request that the Parliament of Canada be very vigilant in ensuring that the CRTC carefully regulates the use of foul language on radio and television.
They indicate that many of their efforts as parents are counteracted by what happens on radio and television. They also underline that it is not necessary to use this kind of language in order to inform or to entertain.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I have a petition from social scientists in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland who are upset, which is perhaps the right way of saying it, with the government's impending decision to merge the SSHRC with the Canada Council.
The petitioners point out that our greatest challenges today are social problems that could be addressed by social scientists. They point out there was no consultation and that the system has worked well since its very beginning. They believe it is a step backward.
They ask that this decision be deferred until consultation takes place.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to present a petition today signed by numerous residents of my riding of Kingston and the Islands, and some residents in Ottawa and Nepean, Ontario.
These Canadians are concerned about the failure of the government to take any steps to eliminate child poverty in Canada. They call upon Parliament to reaffirm and keep its commitment to seek the elimination of poverty among children by the year 2000 and to develop a plan for the implementation of this commitment.
I am sure they join millions of other Canadians in wishing there was an election so they could elect a government which would implement this and present a plan to Parliament to eliminate child poverty by the year 2000 in accordance with the expressed wishes of this House. Unfortunately the current government seems bent on doing nothing and, frankly, as it comes to the end of its mandate, it ought to get out of office and call an election at once.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 36. The petition is being presented on behalf of my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops, and includes the signatures of many residents of Iroquois Falls, Ontario.
The petitioners point out that the goods and services tax is an unfair form of taxation and the they call upon members of Parliament, the Government of Canada and the House of Commons to reject the current goods and services tax and reform the taxation system so that there is an effective minimum tax on wealthy individuals and corporations.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and privilege of presenting a petition primarily from the parishioners of the St. John's Presbyterian Church in Windsor outlining their concern about violence against women and children.
February 2, 1993

They ask Parliament to accept legislation designed to eliminate that violence which, as we all know in this society, is most invidious. They pray that Parliament will act to resolve this problem.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege to present several petitions, all on the goods and services tax, from residents in Saskatoon and in Ontario.
The petitioners point out that the goods and services tax is a particularly unfair tax because it puts an undue burden on those who are less able to pay. They call upon Parliament to reject the current goods and services tax and reform the taxation system so that there is an effective minimum tax on the wealthy and corporations.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a number of petitions from constituents in my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk dealing with the sale and manufacture of killer cards.
The petitioners want the laws of Canada amended to stop the importation of these cards and to let the distributors of these cards in Canada know they will not be tolerated in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a number of petitions pursuant to Standing Order 36.
The first set of petitions deals with the goods and services tax, an issue which is still very much in the minds of the people of Canada.
These petitions are signed by people from all across Canada but interestingly many from the Oshawa area, formerly represented by Mr. Broadbent and at present ably represented in this House by one of my colleagues. The petition calls for a rejection of the goods and services tax and the reform of the tax system in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the second set of petitions were gathered on behalf of the member for Burnaby-Kingsway who has been an advocate for
Routine Proceedings
many years for changes in the Canadian Human Rights Act.
These petitions call for an amendment to the Canadian Human Rights Act to add sexual orientation. As the House will know, a bill has been introduced but the government has still not given any sign of proceeding with it. I would hope this House will listen to the prayers of these petitioners and encourage the government to proceed forthwith with this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and the privilege to table a petition that has been certified correct as to form and content.
It was submitted and signed by Canadian citizens of Armenian origin who remind us that the Quebec National Assembly tabled a similar motion recognizing the importance of the anniversary of the Armenian genocide. I therefore wish to join my colleague from Saint-Laurent-Cartierville, who is actively involved in these issues, as well as several other members but mainly the hon. member for Saint-Laurent-Cartierville, who represents a large segment of this group, as I do, but she is still the leader.
These people have been residents of Canada all their lives, have contributed to Canadian society and earnestly hope that Parliament will continue to express its sympathy to the Armenian people in recognition of what they suffered during the genocide that took place on April 24, 1915, and that Parliament will support international pressures on the Tbrkish government to recognize as factual the terrible events of April 24, 1915.

I have a brief decision to announce on Bill C-98, an act to provide additional borrowing authority for the fiscal year beginning on April 1, 1992.
There are four amendment motions on the Order Paper for report stage of Bill C-98.

Motions Nos. 1 to 4, standing in the name of the hon. member for Essex-Windsor, seek to delete all clauses of the bill. These motions will be grouped for debate and a vote on Motion No. 1 will apply to Motions Nos. 2, 3 and 4. I shall now propose Motions Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 4 to the House.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Motion No. 1
That Bill C-98 be amended by deleting Clause 1.
Motion No. 2
That Bill C-98 be amended by deleting Clause 2.
Motion No. 3
That Bill C-98 be amended by deleting Clause 3.
Motion No. 4
That Bill C-98 be amended by deleting Clause 4.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it might logically be asked why one would attempt at report stage to simply eliminate a piece of legislation coming from the government.
There are two answers to that question. The first answer is that I believe, as do many Canadians across this country, that this government has lost its right to govern the country. This government has turned its back on so many commitments. It has failed to listen to the people. It has reached and exceeded the usual four years that people grant to even the most unpopular government when it is elected. It is now frankly living on borrowed time and is doing so without any sense of commitment, any sense of new ideas, any sense of new directions to put the 1.6 million Canadians who are out of work back into employment.
We have a government which simply does not deserve the right to continue to sit in the seats of power on the front benches on the government side. That is because this government is doing nothing. This government has had a chance for over four years to write its direction and to respond to the concerns of people but it has refused to do so.
Government Orders
Most recently, at what was effectively the four-year mark of this past government, in the economic statement made last December instead of bringing in a plan to get people back to work, it brought in a plan to attack the jobless. Instead of bringing in a plan to do something to make our tax system fairer, it brought in a plan to make it less fair by simply extending the tax exemption of 21-year family trusts virtually indefinitely so as to give perhaps billions of dollars a year to these trusts. We really cannot calculate it because of the lack of information from this government but it is perhaps billions of dollars a year to these tax protected trusts.
That is one reason. The fact is this government has become an illegitimate government. It simply has not got the moral authority in our view to go forward and borrow from the people of Canada and from the rest of the world the billions of dollars which it suggests it is going to borrow with this piece of legislation.
We must also point out that for the average person, for the average family, for the young person in this country the economic crisis continues despite brave announcements from Statistics Canada that the recession is over. The reality is that since Statistics Canada made that announcement the first statistics came out to show that in the most recent month for which we have data this economy in Canada actually declined instead of advanced. Some proof that the recession is over, some proof indeed.
Today we have given to us the final figures of bankruptcies for the year 1992. We see that this government has succeeded with all its brave talk about managing the economy to achieve under its direction the largest level of bankruptcies this country has ever experienced.
I say shame to this government. Shame to a government that speaks about the importance of small business and lets hundreds, thousands of small businesses go under because of the government's poor economic management.
I say shame to a government that talks about its concerns for people and yet has seen in this past year over 76,000 bankruptcies in Canada. We have never had figures like that before. We have never had statistics that have been so dramatic. Even in 1991 the previous year in which the recession was also biting deeply we had fewer bankruptcies than last year. In the most recent month, December, on the basis of which Statistics Canada said the recession was dead there were more bankruptcies than in the previous month.

February 2, 1993
Government Orders
We see absolutely nothing as we look at the economy in front of us that suggests this government has anything to offer, has anything but bankrupt solutions to go with the bankruptcies which it has created and extended throughout this country.
We cannot possibly support this legislation. We cannot support other legislation coming through this House as part of this same economic package from this government.
We cannot support legislation which in fact will leave women frightened and unable to react to sexual harassment in the work place as a result of the cutbacks and the elimination of unemployment insurance support for anybody who leaves a position under such circumstances and cannot prove definitively that sexual harassment was the cause even though it may have been the major factor in what happened to that woman or that man.
We cannot support that. We cannot support this government's plans later this week to create this vast new tax bonanza for Canadians at the top. These are Canadians who have already benefited tremendously from changes that both the Liberals and the Conservatives have brought into our tax system. These changes that the Liberals and Conservatives brought in have created the vast deficits at the federal level which are so dangerous to the future of our country.
This government and the previous Liberal government have created an economic situation which is damaging Canadians across this nation, hurting the future of not just ourselves but our children and our children's children. We in this party will do everything we possibly can to stop this government from being able to proceed.
There is just one act, one action and one decision which this government has the right to take. This government has been in power too long. This government has stopped listening. This government has failed the economy and the people of this country.
The responsibility now exists for this government to call an election, to give the people of Canada the right they have been waiting to exercise for over four years. That is the right to kick this government out and the right to create a new direction in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Gustafson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member states that the government really has no right to continue.
I read here according to The Gazette that Statistics Canada's figures project Ontario's net debt will reach $53 billion by the end of this year. That is a 63 per cent increase in debt in two years. It also speaks about the federal situation in which we have dealt with the debt.
How can the hon. member stand in this House and compare what an NDP government has done in Ontario by increasing the debt? He also said for example that the NDP government is considering tough welfare reform, possibly forcing recipients to take job training or do voluntary work which is a move that one time would have been unthinkable for a socialist government.
How can the hon. member stand in this place and make the statements he has made in view of the reality and the facts of what has been happening with governments run by the NDP?

Mr. Speaker, it is quite true that the New Democratic Party in all three provinces where it has been elected has had to clean up the mess left by previous governments. The Liberals and Conservatives who created the mess chuckle.
The reality in the province of Saskatchewan for instance, from where the hon. member who just spoke comes, is that the banks were very clear that Grant Devine, the previous Conservative premier, had taken the province to bankruptcy.
In the province of Ontario, you may remember-you may not have been perhaps as close to the Ontario situation as some of us who come from there-the Liberal government went into an election and went through an entire election campaign saying: "Yes, we
February 2, 1993

have a deficit from the past, but so far as the present is concerned, we are running with a surplus of $25 million". The new New Democratic government came into office and was told immediately by the very civil servants selected by the Liberal government that the deficit for that year which the Liberals had started was going to be close to $3 billion.
Oh, that is wrong. Mr. Speaker, how can you allow this? How about Ontario?
Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party Government of Ontario has had to clean up this mess. It had to clean it up in Saskatchewan.
They cleaned it up? They tripled it.

It had to clean it up in British Columbia. The reality is at the federal level at this very moment, for every single tax dollar which a Canadian citizen pays, 35 cents is taken out of that dollar to spend on the federal debt created by Liberals and Conservatives.
New Democrats have never run the federal government. In the province of Ontario, for each dollar taken in taxes from the people of Ontario, only 12 cents goes to pay for the debts which exist in that province.
It seems far more responsible to be in a situation where you lead a government and are able to take 88 per cent of the tax revenue and put it to good use than to be in a situation such as the Liberals and Conservatives have created here at the federal level where 65 cents is all that is left out of each tax dollar to actually spend for services and benefits to the people of the country.
Let us hear no more from Conservatives and Liberals about deficit difficulties and New Democrats because what has happened is that Liberals and Conservatives have taken this country nationally to virtual bankruptcy. Frankly, it will be up to New Democrats after the next election to clean up the mess here just as it has been in the provinces.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would love another question, but I have to speak to this amendment.
Government Orders
I sat here and I listened to this give and take between the people across and the hon. NDPs to my left. I heard the gentleman to my left talking about how the Ontario NDP dealt responsibly with the debt in Ontario. I guess my way of dealing with debt and their way of dealing with debt is not quite the same. I always thought that dealing responsibly with debt was eliminating it, not tripling it. Now I do not even know how much bigger it is going to be, but the line we are hearing is that the Ontario deficit will be well in excess of $10 billion. When they took over, despite all the bad things that the Liberals did in Ontario and all the things that of course the glorious NDP did shortly afterward, they were only able to come up with a $3 billion deficit at the end of that one year.
It was actually $2 billion.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Okay, it was actually $2 billion. I stand corrected. All of a sudden we have these people who really know how to deal with deficit and debt trying to tell us how great things will be after they take over. I am very worried about that.
As members can all remember, and I remind Canadians, in 1983-84 in the period leading up to the election of a massive Conservative majority government here in Canada and subsequently, we heard about how Conservatives were going to deal with deficits and debt over and over and over again. They also had all the answers and they were making all these wonderful predictions and all of the other things.
I must admit they were not quite as successful at tackling the debt as the NDP have been in Ontario. I have to admit that. They did not triple it in one or two years. I mean they really did not. I have to give them credit for that. They did double it though in the space of eight years. Perhaps they should be listening to my colleague from the NDP. They might learn how to do it better, I do not know.
That is not my way of dealing with debt and deficits. I of course am very well aware that there is no real easy answer except hard work and trying to create economic growth. One of the ways of tackling debt and deficit is to create more growth within the economy. We have been through some very trying economic times.

February 2, 1993
Government Orders
I read an article in today's Toronto Star by David Crane. I quote from the article:
Pyongyang is the isolated capital of North Korea where politicians and bureaucrats are the last people in the world who still believe in
communism.
Ottawa is not so isolated, but it's probably the last capital in the Western world where politicians and bureaucrats still cling to the idea that free markets by themselves will guarantee full employment and prosperity.
Certainly, that's the view in such citadels of Ottawa power as the Department of Finance, where any idea of an industrial strategy is shot down the instant the words are mentioned.
Fortunately, some provinces are not waiting for Ottawa to tune into the 21st century. Instead, they are actually working together to see what they can do without Ottawa.
This, ladies and gentlemen, is an example of what we have governing this country. Do we wonder why Canadians have lost faith in government? No small wonder. We have a Minister of Finance who in the midst of one of the most terrible years in terms of job losses, high unemployment rates and bankruptcies who on a television program the other day had the nerve to say that we have created the most jobs of any G-7 country. What he neglects to say is that we have also lost more jobs than anybody else and the jobs that the government has created are low paying, part-time jobs that a person is lucky to have.
The Conservatives are tired. They have had it. They have had it with us criticizing them. They have had it with Canadians criticizing them. They have just plain had it. The time is up, ladies and gentlemen. It is time to call an election. They are tired. They deserve a rest. Canadians are very ready to give them that rest. Many of them may retire and lead a very nice restful life after the hectic days of destroying the economy of our country.
I offer them the opportunity, and Canadians will give them the opportunity whenever they say so. Of course, they are still all debating and watching our Prime Minister as he fiddles with his future. He fiddles: "Am I staying? Am I not? Am I staying? Am I not?" It is for them to guess. That preoccupies their minds. They are really busy worrying about whether he is coming or going, but they are not doing anything for Canadians. We can joke about these things but this is very serious. They have created paralysis in Ottawa where the people wait for some direction from this government. Step down. Call an election or try something; anything.
If you have been laid off and are looking for a job you do not want Statistics Canada to tell you: "Oh, by the way, we are out of the recession". Go and see the people who have just lost their jobs. There are many of them everywhere in this country.
Statistics Canada can say there is a slight upturn in the economy. We are very happy with it but what we want to see are jobs. We do not want to see just a slight upturn in the economy. We want to see an upturn where people will be able to get good jobs. We want to see a government that can focus on people. We are witnessing the price of inaction. We must take some action. Any action is better than what has been happening here. I would ask everyone to defeat this bill.
The amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: No, not the amendment, to defeat this bill. I support the amendment because I want to defeat this bill and that is what the amendment will do. I will do anything I can to convince those opposite to step down. I think it is very important that an election be called, and the sooner the better.
Give yourselves a break and vote for the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: If voting for the amendment means that we are going into an election, by all means let us go to it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish I could speak for half an hour today. There is so much one could say in response to my hon. friends opposite. However, I will not do that.
With all due respect I must say this is a phoney debate. It is a waste of taxpayers' money. It is a waste of the House of Commons' time because these amendments, while in order-Mr. Speaker, you must rule them in order because they are in order-are amendments that simply propose to delete the bill and force this House to debate an extra stage on this bill.
What hon. members opposite should do if they are against the bill is simply vote against it. They should simply speak against it and vote against it. By putting frivolous amendments like this, we have an extra stage of debate which is of no benefit to the Canadian people whatsoever. It is a considerable cost to the taxpayer. Let us be perfectly clear about that.
February 2, 1993

My hon. friend from the New Democratic Party says this government has lost its right to govern. Does he not know his basic political science? Does he not know that a mandate in this country is five years? Certainly he should have learned from the former premier of Ontario, Mr. Peterson, that a mandate is five years. The Liberals have learned that lesson.
If one looks back one could chronicle the different circumstances. I remember, for example, that during the last two decades the Liberals had two majority governments. In 1974 and 1979 Mr. Trudeau went five years before calling an election. From 1980 to 1984 Mr. Trudeau went four years and, I believe, seven months, from February until September. Let us not get sucked in by this phoney nonsense about a term being four years.
A term is five years. This country has problems that need to be addressed. Last fall there was an incredible uncertainty in this country with the referendum and the constitutional situation. The last thing this country needed was the uncertainty of an election so let us not deal with that nonsense.
Regarding the economic crisis, my hon. friend from Essex Windsor says: "Woe is me, woe is me, woe is me". This is the essence of this man's conversation every time he stands up in this House. Yet earlier this morning he and I attended a joint meeting of the external affairs, finance and environment committees in which we heard one of the leading officials of the United Nations say: "I find it interesting to come to Canada and hear Canadians talk about how tough it is in Canada when in fact in any other country in the world the people would give anything to trade their problems for the problems of Canadians".
Sure we have problems in this country. Sure the recession has hit us hard. Sure it has hurt individual Canadians and families. One person unemployed is too many. One bankruptcy is too many, but my goodness let us put things in balance.
The fact of the matter is that this is the best place in the world to be. Why is it that this is the country more than any other that people from other countries in the world want to come to? If they listen to my hon. friends
Government Orders
opposite nobody would ever want to come to this country, but I am not sure who listens to my hon. friends opposite, except maybe the media, when they go on about all this nonsense.
I listened to my hon. friend from the Liberal Party talk about debt. There is the pot calling the kettle black. When this government came into office the Liberal Party had left a $38 billion deficit. How much different is that from the $32 billion we have today? The difference is that they had an operating deficit. They were running the country on $16 billion more than they were taking in and they only had $22 billion in debt.
That was 35.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Today this government is running this country in the black. There is a $6 billion surplus on the operating side. Meanwhile the compound interest on the over $200 billion debt, the legacy of the Thideau government to Canadians, has taken us up to a point in excess of $400 billion. By running the country in the black for the last four years this government is returning some of that deficit money and paying down the national debt. Let us stick to the facts and not hear this malarkey opposite about debt and deficit. My goodness, what nonsense.
The bill before the House would be eliminated by the proposals of my hon. friend in the NDP. It provides for the financial needs of the government. Unlike my friends opposite, this government does not like to see the Government of Canada operate on borrowed money. The philosophy of this party is that we should live within our means. That is why we have had a program of deficit reduction, a program, I might say, consistently opposed by my friends opposite who fought against every cost cutting measure of this government: spend, spend, spend.
We have seen what the Ontario New Democratic Party has done. There is an interesting article in The Montreal Gazette today that talks about debt across the country. It notes that in the last two years provincial debt has increased 50 per cent. What do we see in Ontario? We see a 63 per cent increase.
What is the record of this government? This government's debt has increased by 16 per cent. That 16 per cent is too much but it is a hell of a lot better than the 63 per cent the Ontario New Democratic Party has given the people of that province. It is a heck of a lot better than the 50 per cent the provinces from coast to coast have generally given.

Government Orders
It is interesting to note that the only province that has operated consistently in the black for 20 years is the province of Alberta which just happens to have been governed by a Progressive Conservative government during the same time. I suppose that is coincidence.
We need this borrowing authority to keep the affairs of state going. Revenues are down because we have been through a difficult recession.
A Tory induced recession.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
UI and transfer payments are up. They talk about capping the transfer payments, yet Canada Assistance Plan payments and UI payments are up. That is the way we govern.
We have had other precedents. We had a precedent in 1982 when the Liberal government came to this House looking for an $11 billion supplementary borrowing authority.
This is a realistic situation. We have no choice. It is the way we have to go. If this government continues in the way it has we are going to get that debt situation completely under control, and we think that is what Canadians want.
Our friends in the New Democratic Party have offered more spending. More spending means more borrowing and more debt. As the Prime Minister said yesterday, at least the NDP offers something. Our other friends over there have nothing to offer. We heard their leader the other day say: "I am going to scrap the GST. I do not know where I am going to get the money to replace it, but if you elect me I will tell you then in my first budget". How stupid do they think Canadians are? It cannot possibly be the case. Mr. Speaker, I find it ironic that members on the opposite side should stand and applaud their economic record. Let us try to return to the facts because, I put to the House, Canada is in terrible economic shape. Canadians are worried and they have every legitimate right to be worried about our
current economic circumstances and our economic future.
Let us look at the record of the Tories. With respect to our ability to compete in 1989, we were fourth among all OECD countries. We have fallen to eleventh place today. Since 1984, when the Conservatives took over government, the Canadian share of world trade has fallen from 5 per cent of Gross Domestic Product to 4 per cent, a 20 per cent decline. Our trade surplus with other nations during those eight and a half years has gone down $12.4 billion.
I will refer to what is probably the most alarming figure to me in terms of the future for young Canadians and for our ability to sustain high paying, value added jobs in Canada. In 1984 Canada had a high-tech trade surplus of $1 billion. Today we have a deficit in high-tech trade of $30 billion. If that is not a sign of a declining ability to compete and create wealth through innovation in the industries of the future, I do not know what is.
Turning to some more bad news, in 1984 manufacturing accounted for 20 per cent of wealth production in Canada. Today it is down to 17 per cent. We have seen how since the early 1980s Canada's manufacturing productivity has grown at only about half the rate of all G-7 competitors. In other words we are falling behind in our capacity to do what we have to do to sustain a high level of income for Canadians.
This Tory government has told us that it has put the fundamentals in place, that it has given us the fundamentals to compete. The fundamentals are going down and have gone down consistently since 1984 because we are above all else a trading nation: 30 per cent of our wealth comes from trade and exports. If all of these indicators of our ability to compete are going backward under this Tory program of getting the fundamentals right, what hope are we trying to give to our children?
We have seen the results in terms of unemployment. Today 1.6 million Canadians are without jobs and these are just the ones who say they are still in the job market. It does not include the many other Canadians who are so despondent about their prospects of getting a job that they no longer even try to find one. They know those jobs just are not there.
February 2, 1993

Probably even more alarming is the fact that since January 1989 Canada has lost 365,000 or 18 per cent of its manufacturing jobs. This is deindustrialization of the highest order. No Canadian believes what the Tories have been trying to say, that this was simply a result of previous governments in Canada. This government has been in office now and has had control of the reins of power for more than eight years. It has been its responsibility to set the directions.
What we have seen is a decreasing ability to compete globally, a decreasing ability to be productive, and finally the deindustrialization of Canada. The Tories will also say that what is happening in Canada is a result of globalization, international restructuring, and even the world recession, all factors beyond the control of Canadians.
If these apologists for our present sorry plight are correct, how do they answer the following question? If these are factors beyond Canada's control, why is it that during the same period Canada has lost 18 per cent of its manufacturing jobs and the U.S. has lost only 6 per cent of its manufacturing jobs? How do they explain that unemployment in Canada is at 11.5 per cent and in United States unemployment is at 7.3 per cent?
This is not the result of forces beyond our control, beyond the purview of this government's responsibility to Canadians to set an environment in which we can prosper and compete. This is a direct result of policies introduced by this government. This government gave us a made-in-Canada recession. Even many Tories admit that their single-minded economic measures to get inflation under control cost Canada thousands and thousands of jobs and created a made-in-Canada recession. Why else did our recession start before the international recession and why did it have to last longer?
These people deliberately set about to drive up the dollar from the mid-75 cent area to 90 cents at the same time they gave us free trade. That 25 per cent increase in the value of our dollar was a far greater barrier to our export than any of the tariff restrictions that we negotiated out of the United States in terms of increasing our access there.
Government Orders
How can we compete with a 25 per cent added burden over those years on our backs? It was totally unfair. It was totally unrealistic. It was a trade driven policy, an inflation driven policy which the government chose rather than concentrating on what it is we can compete with and how we can get more of those goods into foreign markets so that we can have more and more Canadians working in our plants, factories and service industries which are dependent upon our exports.
Canadians realize that this government has set these policies, that it is responsible for them. This is why Canadians have shown consistently through their polling that these Tories had options, that they could have done things differently but they did not, and that they were wrong.
I only hope in the last gasping breath of this government that it will tiy to reverse its policies and that it will try to deal with some of its long-term problems that it has neglected in the past, such as increasing literacy, creating an educational system that is responsive to our job needs, increasing funding to science and technology and a renewed commitment to research and development.
Can the government not see what it has done? At least, can it not start to change it or say: We will not change it, we will give Canadians a chance to decide and let Canadians go to the polls.

Mr. Speaker, during this debate on the borrowing authority I would like to spend a bit of time talking about the role of the government and its treatment of the Public Service of Canada. The cuts it has undertaken within the safety infrastructure provided by Transport Canada on the coast of British Columbia I feel endangers the lives of Canadians who live and work in that area.
A rather misguided approach by the Auditor General in some of the criticisms of the Canada Coast Guard I believe has led to a number of ill-conceived programs by Transport Canada.
I would like to start with a basic policy of Transport Canada that seems to be a response to the government's demand for cuts in the services provided to the public, to the people who live in the small communities along the coast of British Columbia, on northern Vancouver Island, the west coast of Vancouver Island, probably a line from Gibsons right up to southeast Alaska and beyond, as it moves up the east side of the panhandle in British Columbia. It is my opinion and the opinion of many

Government Orders
British Columbians that this area is very poorly serviced when it comes to transportation safety infrastructure.
Transportation safety is not the responsibility of ships at sea, of privately operated aircraft, commercial aircraft or of locally organized search and rescue groups of various types, whether they be the marine search and rescue group that is under the sponsorship of the Coast Guard or the volunteer air search and rescue group or the ground search and rescue parties. These people do an enormous job and are a tremendous service to their communities. It must be remembered that in that area, the prime deliverer of transportation infrastructure services is the Government of Canada.
Probably the primary one is the helicopter service out of CFB Comox. For years that service has been totally inadequate. They have some of the best trained crews in the world. They have some of the best equipment in the world, contrary to what the Minister of National Defence and this government would like us to believe. It is my understanding from discussions with people who work at the base, who maintain those aircraft, that the airframe of the Labrador helicopter never wears out. If it is refitted properly and fitted with proper engines, it is one of the most stable vehicles to work with, especially in mountainous terrain.
The problem with the helicopters at CFB Comox is that they have in some instances a two-hour callout time. A member of the Billie family of Comox drowned off Quadra Island. Apparently the boat caught fire. The base, which is about six minutes flying time away, could not get a helicopter out there within two hours. It is absolutely useless if you cannot deliver a primary search and rescue vehicle into that area within a shorter period of time when the base is that close.
In the United States, in southeast Alaska and in the state of Washington, they operate on a totally different principle. Their helicopters are ready to go immediately. There are crews on site. They fire up their machines and they are gone. That is the kind of service that is needed on the coast of British Columbia. It is the kind of service that every British Columbian has to a right to expect, as they do in other areas of Canada.
Ultimately the government has decided that the saving of money is more important than human lives or a legitimate attempt to rescue and save human lives. That is an absolutely clear statement. The example of the Billie family drowning off a fish boat off Comox is a clear example. There are also others.
One of the great things that Transport Canada and the Department of National Defence brag about is the tremendous job they do and the assistance they were able to render to the Princen Dam which was a cruise ship which caught fire off Prince Rupert and southeast Alaska. They were absolutely blind lucky that there was not a storm blowing and that it was not the middle of winter. They could never have reached the ship in a situation like that.
The reverse situation occurred with the sinking of the freighter Lee Wang Zin off that area. By the time you leave Comox, if you get the report after twelve o'clock, you cannot reach that area in daylight hours. The distribution of equipment, callout times and a whole host of other money saving initiatives of the government make sure that the safety equipment is not delivered in a period of time that is useful for searching and for saving lives.
Let us put aside the saving of money in areas that endanger human lives. I say that is completely unacceptable. The helicopters at CFB Comox should be distributed along the coast in a more effective fashion so that those extremely well trained, dedicated crews and that upgraded equipment can be delivered to people in a timeframe which is meaningful. Otherwise we might as well not even have them arrive in time.
Transport Canada had decided that it too was going to get into the saving of money in response to the government's demand. If it had to save money by endangering human life, so be it. It got some solace from the Auditor General who I think in a very misguided fashion said: Let us close all the lighthouses on the coast of British Columbia.
Those lighthouses have provided safety services to mariners, aviators, tourists and people in the commercial marine environment for years and years. Contacts were made and the lines of communication were opened even though they were not formally established. Because some of those lighthouse keepers were not provided with radios, they bought their own so that they could talk to
February 2, 1993

passing ships, give weather reports about local sea conditions in the area and advice on what was happening. They provided that service.
On a large number of occasions, the lighthouse keepers effected their own rescues. They bought their own boats.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order I have been listening with great interest to my hon. friend. We are speaking on an amendment which would delete borrowing authority from the government and deny cash resources.
Can my hon. friend tie in his remarks to taking financial resources from the government. Would that enable the government to do what he is advocating?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am not sure that is a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, what affects the area that I represent, 300 miles of the coast of British Columbia, affects the south coast of Nova Scotia where five fishermen drowned recently.
I am sure the hon. member is interested in exactly the same points I raise. This is affected by borrowing authority and the way we go about it. Borrowing authority involves the money of the Government of Canada and that money should be spent in areas that are extremely relevant. Perhaps he would be prepared to listen to the remarks and I will draw them together to make the relevant point that he is concerned about.
If I could return to these remarks, the policy of Transport Canada and the Auditor General in scrutinizing the funding of the Government of Canada has led to an impression in Transport Canada that there should be cuts to the lighthouse services. The point I was making is that those lighthouse services provide an important safety service to the people of British Columbia.
Those people have affected rescues and they are not provided with vessels to do that. They are not provided with training and they are not provided with proper equipment. When somebody is in a desperate situation and in danger of losing his or her life and the lives of their family members, there is no choice. Names have been submitted and forwarded in the hope that these lighthouse keepers can be given the Canada 125 medal in recognition of the tremendous service they have provided in an isolated environment without resources.
Government Orders
The government finally talked to people in the field including mariners, aviators, tourists and commercial users of the service. They have been told not to cut out those lighthouse services but to upgrade them so they can provide weather reports, radio contacts and provide them their own vessels.
As a result, the Coast Guard turned around and did a study. It was called "The Future Use of Lighthouses Report" and made some very positive recommendations: not shutting down the lighthouses, providing them with radios, providing them with some training for giving weather broadcasts, which is absolutely the most crucial need.
When one gets so far up the coast of British Columbia, one cannot leave without a weather report. One cannot get a decent weather report because they are not provided. Only the lighthouses do and they are so sketchy they are hardly useful. "The Future Use of Lighthouses Report" stated these people should be given the skills they need and the equipment they need to get this rolling. Now they are under the gun again.
I would just like to draw the conclusion together. The government has also cut back fire-fighting services at Port Hardy Airport. It has done it with flight service stations. It has done it with the closure of Bull Harbour, the closure of the Cape St. James lighthouse. It is talking about removing the hovercraft from Parksville. Ultimately that involves endangering human life. We cannot tolerate the removal of these infrastructures.

Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker for the New Democratic Party, the member for Essex-Windsor I believe, was making the point that this government has no legitimacy to carry on because it is so low in the polls. I think the member's question missed the point. Obviously he was not paying much attention to my speech. The point I was trying to make is that even beyond politics there is a far more important issue. That is the responsibility we all have to protect human life. This government's financial cuts to the Public Service and what it has done to a dedicated group of people by completely demoralizing them, has created a tremendous amount of uncertainty. To the government, saving cash is more important than serving people, even if it is to save its own life.
For the benefit of the hon. member from the Liberal Party I mentioned the question of removing the hovercraft from Parksville, the shutting down of the Cape St. James lighthouse, the closure of lighthouses, the closure of the Bull Harbour lifeboat station, the purchase of inappropriate but certainly cheaper equipment, the failure to end the callout time so that crews are on site at CFB Comox and are able to depart immediately with well-trained crews and good equipment. [DOT]'
All of this really seems to stem from a much greater concern about saving money rather than saving people. That is what I think is going to be the end of the Conservatives.
I should point out that the closure of the lighthouse stations and the shut-down of many of the search and rescue equipment was the fault of the previous Liberal government. Otto Lang, a previous Minister of Transport, was one of the most serious offenders against concern for the lives of people who work on the west coast and I am sure the east coast as well. Mr. Speaker, I want to lead off in this debate by making a few preliminary comments on some statements that were made that I certainly would like to clarify for the benefit of anybody watching the debate here this morning.
First of all, the penultimate speaker from the NDP said they would not really know about deficits and all that sort of stuff because federally they have never been in power. I would suggest that if they continue going the way they are going right now they will never be in power. I think this was a precursor to some of the concerns that they have. When people are frustrated they lash out. Therefore I take a certain amount of what the NDP say about my party's record with an understanding of their frustration at never forming the government.
My good friend the Conservative member for South Shore was accurate in one sense when he said that the Conference Board forecasted that Canada would grow
3.3	per cent this coming year. I cannot quarrel because that is what it said, although whether or not it happens is another thing. What he did not mention is that it also said that we would have the highest unemployment rate among the G-7 countries, except for Italy, at 11.3 per cent. Italy will have 11.5 per cent and Canada will have
11.3	per cent.
The whole point of this discussion, the whole point of the government's attempt to get its act together, and the whole point of one of the things that we have been doing with our platform is to try to get jobs back in this country and to get people working.
I come from a riding where not many people are working as a result of mismanagement of the fisheries, poor employment opportunities and a litany of other things that I have talked about in this House, as have other members from Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada. I am not here to reiterate those things. I will be doing that at a later time.
I want to more closely examine the over-all context of what we are discussing this morning, which is the government's business of borrowing money to run the country. The Tories are stretching their credibility when they continue after eight and half years in power to blame another government, whatever government it is. It happens to be the party that I represent. To continue
February 2, 1993

year after year with the same litany of excuses is not only irresponsible but it shows that they are giving little importance and little credibility to the intelligence of the viewers who hear this litany. People would have to be very dedicated Conservatives to really believe all these things.
I like to deal in facts and figures. It is good to be qualitative from time to time but it is very difficult to argue with the facts and figures which are available to any member. Nobody can dispute them. They are available.
When this government came into power in 1984 there was a certain debt and a deficit. The deficit was $38 billion. After eight and a half years in power, 33 tax increases and after saying in every budget that the name of the game was to reduce the deficit the government has not reduced the deficit much. This was at a time when the economy was growing. In the first four years this government was in power the economy of the world, and particularly the economy of Canada, was buoyant and the government had an opportunity to reduce the deficit as it kept promising to do budget after budget.
What was the government doing? Program spending was increasing at the rate of 4 per cent a year. The government talked about cutting the deficit by increasing taxes, although it never really talked too much about increasing taxes. The government talked about reducing the debt. Yet every year the government would increase its spending by 4.1 per cent, which is the average over the last eight and a half years, and the interest on the annual deficit grew at 9 per cent, which is about three times the rate of growth of the economy. If it does that in periods of growth and a good economy and it cannot control the deficit what on earth is it going to do in a recession or depression?
The government has run out of tools. It has run out of tricks. It has taxed the middle class, sometimes at the expense of the rich, sometimes at the expense of corporations and sometimes at the expense of certain business interests, to the point where the middle class cannot pay any more.
Government Orders
The interest payments on the debt when the Tories came to power in 1984 totalled $27.5 billion. It is double that today. Yet they say it is the fault of the Liberals.
Where have the taxes gone? Of the $122 billion that was taken in by this government to run the country, which is the subject we are talking about today, 50 per cent came from income taxes. The middle class pays most of the income tax. Twelve per cent was from the goods and services tax, which is the most hated and most unique tax in the world. Thirteen per cent came from UI contributions, to which the government no longer contributes and so it comes from the working class, the middle class, and business. Thirty-seven per cent came from sin taxes on gas, alcohol, cigarettes and those kinds of items and 8 per cent came from corporations.
I regret that I have not been able to get the exact figures for 1984. I have been told by the research effort that I was able to mount yesterday and today that if we include the GST the ratio paid by the middle class compared to other classes is 60:40. In 1984 it was more like 40:60. It has reversed. The middle class proportionately is paying almost double what it was paying before.
Economists agree on very little but one thing they do agree on is that we cannot just talk about the debt we must talk about growth as well.
The amount of goods and services, of anything that is worth anything that is produced in this country is the Gross Domestic Product, which is essentially what we earn as a country. Our debt is what is owed as the national debt.
The ratio of one to the other in 1984 was 46.4 per cent. In other words our debt was 46 per cent of what we produced. It is as if an individual earned x dollars and would be paying 46.4 per cent of everything he or she was worth on interest payments.
That figure has gone up 30 per cent. In other words the ratio of Gross Domestic Product to debt is now 62.7 per cent. That is an incredible rise. In other words an individual owes 62.7 per cent interest on what he or she has borrowed as an individual. That means an individual would have less than 40 per cent of his or her income to spend on delivering the goods, on raising a family, on sending kids to university and everything else.

Government Orders
More important, that individual is worse off by 30 per cent than she or he was eight and a half years ago. Would that individual blame that on somebody else? One would have to take responsibility for that oneself.
In the closing moments of my presentation I must mention one thing that has arisen in my riding time after time, and I am about to meet with the community. At a time when spending has been increased by 4 per cent and people are being taxed they feel they are not getting value for their money.
One of the areas that has been of great concern in my party and for a lot of my constituents is the way in which rural people have been treated with respect to postal services. In 1986 this government came up with a plan to reduce 10,000 people and 3,221 post offices in rural areas. It has done so despite countless speeches in this House, tens of thousands of people presenting petitions, admonitions, letters to ministers, and meetings at town halls. I cannot tell the House the number that I have attended. I am about to attend another one in a couple of weeks time. The community is very concerned that it is paying all these taxes and it is not getting the postal service that it feels it should get.
I am particularly concerned about this because about 83 per cent of those who work in the post office are female. There is great concern about jobs for the female part of our population and that is another concern.
I have given just one example but it is a universal example that concerns people. Quite frankly the government has no right to be proud of its record and it should be very much ashamed of where it has us today.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on this borrowing bill which arises out of the mini budget that the government brought down in the fall. It really outlines the direction this government wants to take our economy in the next few years, before an election in the fall.
Neither I nor the people in my riding support the economic direction in which this government has been taking the country. This country is really facing an economic crisis. There are 1.6 million Canadians out of
work and many of those Canadians reside in my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk.
The government talks about economic growth. As the hon. member said earlier, it plans for 3 per cent economic growth. However in all those discussions the government does not talk about jobs. Although it talks about economic growth it hides the fact that even though we will have economic growth over the next few years no more jobs will be created.
The government likes to talk about competitiveness, saying proudly that we will grow. However it says to the unemployed Canadian or the unemployed person from Haldimand-Norfolk, for example in the steel industry, that there will be no jobs for steel workers who are being laid off because Canadian steel is being unduly and unfairly attacked by our counterparts to the south.
This government made a commitment during the free trade debate that our steel industry would have open access to the American market. As we have seen over the last few weeks, this has not been the case. The government does not seem to be prepared to do anything about it.
There are no jobs for fanners in this economic statement. Farmers are devastated by low commodity prices and must deal with a government that does not seem to want to represent them internationally. It does not seem to want to stand up against the unfair trading practices of the Europeans and our neighbours to the south who constantly use export enhancement to send grain that should have been Canadian into our previous markets.
Farmers in the supply managed areas of dairy and poultry are extremely concerned about this government's representation of them at the GATT negotiations and the way in which this government has caved in at the negotiations with regard to its position on article XI.
There are no jobs for our youth. Youth unemployment is at 19 per cent. Canadian youth, whether in Vancouver, Montreal or my own riding of Haldimand-Norfolk, see no hope for their future. They do not see an economic plan that gives them a chance for a job, or even a chance to become trained and to be able to compete for these new jobs that the government talks about.
February 2, 1993

I and the former youth critic, the member for York North, travelled across this country and talked to young people about their hopes and about their needs if they are to compete in this changing economy. We found a real lack of hope. In many cases it seemed that young people have given up because they have been faced with a government that seems not to have listened to their ideas for economic change.
A few weeks ago we presented alternatives to the Canadian public. We presented future directions that we thought the government might take and future directions that we as a government will take in order to include young people in this economic plan, in the economic future of our country. We hope to be able to present these ideas in a general election, which hopefully will be sooner than later.
We can no longer put blame on past governments. I sat here listening to the government blaming the provinces, the NDP blaming the Liberals and the government blaming the Liberals for our economic woes. The time for blame has stopped. The time to take action is now. I wish that hon. members on all sides of the House would quit blaming each other and get on with the action that is needed. I know it is easy to criticize. As a member of the Official Opposition, my role in may ways is to criticize government policy. We do that in order to try to keep this government responsible and keep it aware of the problems being faced by ordinary Canadians. At the same time we must be willing to offer solutions and alternatives. I am sure my hon. friends across the way were listening very closely when my leader gave a speech last week at the University of Ottawa, which was very widely accepted by the young people there, outlining alternatives, the Liberal's position and the directions we would like to take this country economically.
My leader, I thought, outlined very clearly the alternatives we would be bringing forward in an election and those are the directions we would be moving in once we became government.
The simple fact is, as my leader said, we have to make economic growth and job creation the top priorities in this country. We cannot have economic growth without jobs. Strangely, these days we seem to hear from the gentlemen across and from many Canadians how we have to become competitive. However, we must be
Government Orders
willing to build a more highly educated and skilled work force. This government is not giving Canadians the tools which would enable them to compete globally.
It talks about competitiveness but at the same time it does not talk about how Canadians can be competitive and where these jobs are for Canadians to compete in. In order to be competitive we have to put Canadians back to work. We have to be able to meet these so-called global challenges of the 21st century. We must be committed to new initiatives to promote labour force training, research and development and marketing support. Ultimately, as I heard when I was at the University of Calgary last week, this country must be committed to education.
Unfortunately, nothing in this government's economic policies and the economic statement by the minister really outlined in any meaningful way any sort of government commitment. It just promised to fulfil old promises and make new ones while sneaking in cuts on the side. Canadians can see through these empty promises and they are not going to buy them any more.
One thing I have learned since I have been here over the last four years is that government really needs to regain the confidence of Canadians. I do not mean the government across but we as parliamentarians need to regain this confidence or else this economy will not build. I believe the way to regain this confidence is to show them a direction, show them they are important as individuals and give them the tools that are necessary for them in order to compete in this changing economy. Those tools include training and retraining. That is why my leader has announced a co-operative program in which governments, businesses, educators and all involved in this process work together to give not only our youth but all unemployed Canadians an opportunity to be able to compete.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today as a member of Parliament from Saskatchewan on the second sitting day of Parliament in 1993, exactly one week, seven days after 12,000 to 15,000 farmers and concerned Saskatchewan residents rallied in Saskatoon to bring to this government's attention their desperate situation. That rally with that many people strongly indicates that their call for help is not idle chatter. Their situation is very serious. Their situation is serious and demands immediate attention.

Government Orders
It points out that 1993 will be one of the most challenging years that Canadians have ever witnessed. Certainly it will be one of the most challenging years that Saskatchewan people have ever witnessed or will have to go through.
When we look at what the agenda is for this government in 1993, we see an incredible amount of attention regarding issues that directly affect Saskatchewan people. We see possible changes to the Canadian Wheat Board, the transportation system for agricultural production, a desperate need for a third line of defence funding and deficiency payments that have not been met for two to three years.
We see changes to the way in which credit will be offered by this government to farm people and residents of rural Saskatchewan. We see changes to the supply management system being negotiated at the GATT that will be a direct threat to many of the residents of rural Saskatchewan.
While those are related to agricultural issues, the people of Saskatchewan also face the same challenges that other Canadians will be faced with as well. There is the continuing attack on them from an unfair taxation system and a North American free trade agreement that is threatening jobs and the security of Canadians from coast to coast. The disputes that concern steel, pork, fish and other matters in our fight with the United States are also matters that will greatly affect the people of Saskatchewan.
I want to bring a number of matters directly to the attention of this government during the course of debate on this bill in which the government is asking permission to borrow more money to carry on with more of the same failed programs and policies that it has had over the last few years.
At that Saskatchewan rally the producers had a number of important things they wanted this government to hear. It was not just a matter of the need for immediate cash, but that was certainly what prompted many of those people to be there. The farm crisis is quite desperate. The numbers are quite overwhelming, indicating that without deficiency payments for the last two years, Saskatchewan producers are already behind $1 billion to $1.5 billion of where they would be if there was
a fair trading system in this country and this world related to agricultural products.
Deficiency payments, a third line of defence payment, is a very immediate need of Saskatchewan producers, an industry that is very important to this country, to all of the people who live here, whether they are in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Halifax or St. John's. The crisis in agriculture affects all of us.
The first message out of that farm rally was that we have to get some cash into the hands of the Saskatchewan producer immediately. The producers went much further than that, indicating that we have a long-term problem. Obviously if we have a problem now it is because existing programs have failed us dismally.
The first year of the 1991 GRIP program has just ended. It is that program which has helped to produce the shortfall in cash that we have on the farm today. We can project that there will be further decreases in agricultural income over the course of the 1993 crop year that will result from the 1992 GRIP program but the current crisis is related to the existing program that was put in place by this government in agreements with the provincial governments prior to 1991.
We have to correct the long-term program as well. That long-term program is a very important one for all those producers who can survive the immediate financial crisis that we have now.
There were other matters that the producers raised at the farm rally that I want to bring to the attention of this government. The overwhelming majority of those 12,000 to 15,000 producers had four other important things they wanted to say to this government.
The first one is very specific: Oats must be put back under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. This government must maintain and enhance the powers of the Canadian Wheat Board because it is the only way that Canadians are going to have the opportunity and the ability to stay involved in the international marketplace in the long term. This government is contemplating removing barley from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, leaving only wheat under its jurisdiction.
The message from that farm rally was very clear. They want barley maintained under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. Under no circumstance should barley be taken out from the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board.
February 2, 1993

There are two very important messages from that farm rally right off the bat. They do not want cash just today. In the long term they enhanced and strengthened powers of the Canadian Wheat Board. Keep barley there and put oats back under the jurisdiction.
Therefore, the Canadian Wheat Board has to be our central desk selling method, which is a very important matter. This government is contemplating changes to the way in which grain is transported from the farm gate through the elevator system to the ports.
The Western Grain Transportation Act has certain guarantees to producers. The government wants to change that. It indicated after talks across the prairies last year that it is seriously considering changes.
The message from that farm rally in Saskatchewan is do not change the method of payment. Maintain the Western Grain Transportation Act, the Crow benefit and if nothing else, ensure that all Saskatchewan producers are treated fairly in the method of payment by ensuring that the status quo is maintained. That was a very important message that came out of that farm rally.
When this government talks about looking at its programs and policies and ensuring that it is looking after the interests of the Canadians it is supposed to represent, it has to take those messages into account. These are very important matters to Saskatchewan producers. We cannot forget that many of the problems on the prairies are a direct result of the continual off-loading of federal government problems on to the provinces.
The Canadian government has a minister of grains and oilseeds. At one point the grain sector was a national responsibility. In 1988, 100 per cent of farm programs relating to grain and problems like the drought that affects the farm situation were carried by Ottawa. The financing was carried by Ottawa. Today only 57 per cent of agricultural support is carried by Ottawa.
Saskatchewan, with 40 per cent of the farms and 4 per cent of the population, is having to carry the costs of 47 per cent of those farm support programs for which Ottawa just four years ago had 100 per cent responsibility.

We have to find ways of ensuring that the national dollar is directed at some of these resource based economies. I, speaking as a Saskatchewan member of Parliament, spoke directly about grains and the agricultural sector. I know my colleagues can talk about fisheries and other resources based economies from their parts of the world.
I have one last point as far as Saskatchewan is concerned. I attended the Saskatchewan Urban Municipalities convention yesterday in Saskatoon. The premier of our province indicated that agricultural support is costing every single Saskatchewan taxpayer $200. The Government of Canada that taxpayers support is just $20. Saskatchewan is paying its way. It is time that Ottawa supported the work of all Saskatchewan producers in an industry in desperate straits.

Mr. Speaker, last year the Minister of Finance presented us with a budget that did absolutely nothing to revive the economy. The Conservatives' financial measures have once again overlooked all those Canadians who are without work today and probably will be without work for a very long time; 1.6 million people are unemployed, and it goes on.
Where are the retraining programs for all these people who want to work? Where are the job creation programs? The Conservative government seems to be short of ideas, short of initiative and especially short of creativity. It is doing nothing, absolutely nothing, to put Canada back to work. That is not how one builds a strong, competitive economy. Above all, it is not the way to be seen as a great nation in this period of increasing globalization.
This government is really good at making promises that it regularly forgets to keep. How can our young graduates hope to fulfil their dreams and ambitions if they are unemployed when they graduate and have to pay back their student debts? How will our adults and, unfortunately, many of our teenagers who are illiterate or barely literate survive in our society if no program is being considered and given priority? How will this 40 per cent of the population overcome this problem?
This government seems to have forgotten all those who have major economic problems, all those who can no longer make ends meet. How will children living in poverty be able to develop physically and mentally if they are not healthy and educated?
In 1991, 700,000 children lined up at food banks. Is that acceptable? Is that right in a country which is supposed to be rich in resources? How can these children escape their predicament if their parents do not find work?
To quote my colleague from Willowdale who said in another speech: "Canadians were counting on this government to give new direction to the economy in order to help with a real recovery. Their decision to stay the course does nothing for the 1.6 million unemployed Canadians who are looking for work, to say nothing of those on welfare".
Canadian small business people who have been going bankrupt at an increasing rate get only crumbs which are barely enough to keep up with inflation. The measures taken to control cross-border shopping do not seem to be enough to stem the flow of millions of dollars to the United States. There is nothing to reassure Canadians about their economic future.

The Conservatives simply do not care about average Canadians. They simply have not been listening to their constituents who are desperately seeking relief from these tough Tory times. Canadians are asking for this government to listen for a change. They want a federal government to lead them to economic stability and security. This is a fundamental argument for national unity. Economic instability in Canada only fuels the drive for sovereignty. That is why we must find a way to get Canada working again.
What I find incredible about the Conservatives is that the amount of money allocated for training adjustment has been cut by $110 million. It is incredible that at a time when 1.6 million Canadians are out of work this government is doing absolutely nothing. We are borrowing money to increase the debt. That is either cowardice on the part of the Conservative government or intellectual bankruptcy.
The Liberal Party is ready to meet this challenge. That is why my colleagues and I cannot wait for the writs to be issued and an election to be called. We will offer the people of this country a real alternative, one that is compassionate and understanding, one that will listen to Canadians, and an alternative that will provide the poor and the unemployed with the tools they need to be active, to prosper and to regain pride and confidence not only in themselves but in the country in which they live.
The Conservatives, fearing an attack from the ideological right, are cutting the programs that have helped build Canada. They want to co-op the Reform Party's agenda because they have no ideas of their own.
The cuts to ministers' salaries and the proposal to eliminate first-class travel in Canada that only existed for a few special ministers of this government were largely symbolic. This government really hurts average Canadians by cutting back on certain agencies that give Canadians non-partisan advice and alternatives in such areas as economic and scientific policy. In an astounding move the government eliminated the Science Council.
February 2, 1993

Canada is trying to become the world leader in science and technology. It is trying to leave behind the attachment it has had to the exploitation of the environment, and this government is blocking that progress. This action is counterproductive and will limit Canada's ability to be competitive in the global market.
As the Official Opposition spokesperson on multicul-turalism and citizenship I must comment on the government's cuts in this area. It is absolutely shameful this government is welshing on a promise made to the Canadian Japanese community. The Canada Race Relations Foundation, which this budget shelves indefinitely, was announced as part of the Japanese Canadian redress settlement. The foundation was established with a grant of $24 million, $12 million of which was donated on behalf of the Japanese Canadian community in commemoration of the suffering of Japanese Canadians during World War II.
The Conservative government, which during the last election claimed to support multiculturalism and made a promise that it would do something about it has made a complete about-face by shelving both the Race Relations Foundation and the Heritage Language Institute. The Conservatives are reneging on two-thirds of their legislative commitment to multiculturalism. At a time when intolerance and bigotry are on a rise throughout the world the federal government should be contributing more rather than less to this program.
The final issue I would like to raise is that of the cancellation of the Court Challenges Program. We have talked about it before. It is reprehensible that this Conservative government would remove funding, and thereby access to the courts, for people who need protection under the charter of rights by cutting the budget on this program and then borrowing again to increase the debt. The government is attacking the rights of citizens to challenge present and future legislation that unjustly infringes on the rights of Canadians. If this government still believes in the principle of equality of the individual, I urge it to reverse this decision and reinstate the Court Challenges Program.
