This government's economic and social agenda simply does not reflect the real needs of Canadians. It is something that the vast majority of my constituents and I oppose. It is time for new ideas and new alternatives. The Liberal Party is ready to give them.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on behalf of the constituents of York West to speak to this borrowing bill which is one of the centrepieces emanating from the recent budget presented to this House and to this country.
One gets the feeling, and it cannot be helped, that through serious and long-standing economic turbulence this government and the Conservative Party opposite simply prefers to put on the automatic pilot and pretend that economic turbulence does not exist.
This latest parliamentary pause was long enough for members of Parliament to enjoy their families and certainly enjoy the benefit of touching base with their constituents in their ridings to try to get the pulse of a country. They will try, as best as they can, to reflect that pulse, that concern, those aspirations and those dreams in this place.
Members on the government benches should have talked to Canadians about their taxes, about the GST, about the record number of unemployed that is reaching almost two million Canadians, and about the fact that with their policies they prefer very much in a bravado sense to attack the unemployed rather than to attack unemployment.
They should have stopped to think about the consequences of the trade deal and the impact it is having on our work force and on some of our key sectors, as witnessed recently by the attack on our steel industry. They should have talked to the increasing number of people who have to rely on welfare or other social assistance programs or the growing number of people in the line-ups at food banks.
If they cared to talk to Canadians about these concerns they would transmit a message to the country through Parliament that they were willing to change, that they were willing to modify, that they were willing to minimize the hurt, that they were willing to admit without fear of being uncourageous or shamed that a number of

February 2, 1993
Government Orders
policies had not worked, and that they were prepared to change course.
We would have thought, if they cared about real Canadians and their families in the regions, the cities and the farms in all our constituencies, they would not have put Parliament on automatic pilot and that they would not have put shutters on and pretended that things were proceeding in a very hopeful and enthusiastic way, because they are not.
It is not because we on this side of the House enjoy the litany of statistics or of causes that we quote. No one takes pleasure in talking about those problems, but it is the responsibility of governments, legislators and elected representatives to solve those concerns and to solve those problems on behalf of a nation. It is not the responsibility of this House to be insignificant or indifferent to what is going on in real Canada.
Canadians in greater numbers are beginning to be indifferent and cynical toward our institutions because they do not believe, when they turn on their television sets, that we are anchored in reality. They do not believe that they make a difference. They do not believe that their concerns are being heard. If they are not being heard, how can those concerns and problems be addressed?
We are discussing the remnants of a budget that is already antiquated. It is not working. It is not addressing the concerns we see day in and day out.
Rather than presenting the traditional budget during the month of February which has been a long-standing practice we have a knee-jerk reaction by the government and Minister of Finance to postpone the budget. We have a knee-jerk reaction to postpone the throne speech which would have set a new course and created a new agenda. Why postpone a budget and a throne speech? Because the Tories are engaged in a navel-gazing exercise, trying to decide who should be the captain at the automatic pilot controls at the front of the plane. The country is becoming subservient to this exercise.
I submit, and other colleagues have been suggesting, that the country deserves better. It is not that any one party is holier than thou. It is not that any one party is perfect and has all the answers. We must strive to find those answers.
We are dumbfounded that the Conservative Party and government opposite have failed so miserably in even recognizing that hurt, that pain and that desire for
economic stimulation, for economic change, for economic renewal, for economic assistance, for economic hope and for economic confidence.
You cannot go into your riding without discussing with people the economic climate of the day. It is a strait-jacket on our country. It is a strait-jacket on both the young and on the old, on those who are working and those who are unemployed. It is a strait-jacket that prevents us from being what we can be. We want to help this government and this country in shedding that strait-jacket.
We marvel that this place has become so insignificant. It does not speak to the problems of Canadians who wake up early in the morning to get on with life and who are speaking to us in our offices or our churches or our school gymnasiums or wherever we meet them.
No connection.

There is not, as my friend from Broadview-Greenwood says, a connection. That is why people are indifferent and cynical about this institution. It is not our institution, it is theirs. This is the forum of Canadians. Therefore we eagerly anticipate the election that is coming.
Canadians during the Christmas and New Years break, after they wished you the best, eagerly suggested that judgment day is approaching or that finally 1993 is here. It is the people, not the Liberal opposition or the New Democratic Party, who have finally concluded that the only way this place will once again be connected to their concerns is by allowing them to exercise their judgment on election day.
It is for the people to set the agenda and a future government to pursue that agenda with vigour, with honesty and with a sense of compassion. We have a parliamentary majority which amounts to a parliamenta-iy dictatorship. The shutters are on. The automatic pilot is on. The turbulence continues and people are hurting. It is time this came to an end.

Mr. Speaker, as we debate this bill which allows the government to borrow more and more money I cannot help but get the image of the interchangeability between Bay Street and the House of Commons, particularly on the opposite side. I have this image of the Campeau Corporation and I have this image of Olympia & York. There are many other examples. Of course they are examples of the abject failure of the neo-conservative, monetarist theory which this government is so hell-bent on following and
February 2, 1993

has been following so assiduously ever since it got elected in 1984. With the interchangeability of it, I guess I am in a bit of a conundrum as to whether we should be saying there but for the grace of God go the people who would have trashed the Campeau Corporation and Olympia & York. I suppose if one was on Bay Street, one would say there but for the grace of God go the people who have trashed the Government of Canada and Canada as a whole.
It is no wonder, as many other members have stated, the Canadian public is absolutely distressed with us as politicians. The Canadian public is cynical about the institute of Parliament. I would like to confess to the public of Canada right now that I certainly join them in that. I do not blame them for being cynical about politicians. I have certainly become cynical myself.
We have a government which was elected in 1984 with all kinds of promises: jobs, jobs, jobs. We have a government that was re-elected in 1988, when I came into this House of Commons, with the promise that with the free trade deal with the United States this country would go into prosperity like we had never seen before.
What I have seen is that we have become impoverished as a nation because of these monetarist theories that they have been so firmly following. I as a working person can relate very well to the majority of Canadians. I have a bit of trouble relating to those from Bay Street, but I can certainly relate to those who do not come from Bay Street.
My memory is that in the late seventies and early eighties we were a prosperous nation before the previous government brought in wage and price controls, before it brought in six and five. It was going to fight inflation to the ground. It did not work, but that is beside the point. It did not work. This government which came in on the heels of a very unpopular government was going to turn things around. Of course it made it worse in spades.
I do not want to dwell too much on that. I want to address a few of the specifics of what has happened in this country, particularly under this government. I come from Saskatchewan. Other members of my caucus have spoken about the farm situation. Certainly the province of Saskatchewan, not to exclude the provinces of Manitoba or Alberta, is in dire straits.

While the member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake was speaking one member, I think from Willow-dale, was laughing. He thought it was rather funny that we were sitting here talking about oats and barley. I guess he really could not relate to anything that went on in agriculture.
I would like to remind anyone who is watching and I certainly would like to remind the members opposite and those to my right as well-I know there are some people in the Liberal caucus very knowledgeable of the farm situation, but some of them obviously are not and can certainly stand some education along those lines-as well as the Canadian public, those who do not have anything to do with farming, those who think that there is no relationship between themselves and the agricultural people of this land, of this thought.
If you eat, you are involved in agriculture. It is high time that everyone in Canada took notice of that, paid attention to it and realized that the people in the agricultural communities of this country, whether they are growing grain, potatoes or apples, certainly do make a contribution to this country. If they do not succeed, the rest of us suffer enormously because of that.
I made reference earlier to the free trade agreement with the United States and how it was supposed to bring prosperity. It certainly has not brought prosperity to Canadian farmers. Our present government has made only a shadow of an effort, if it can even be given that much credit, of trying to defend our agricultural community in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade negotiations.
Aside from that, under the free trade agreement there is a clause which says specifically that in this instance- unlike the General Agreement on Tariffs and Tirade where there are 108 countries, the free trade agreement with the United States has only two countries, little Canada and the gigantic United States-neither country will use any kind of practice which would in traditional trading areas be to the detriment of the other country.
The main problem that agricultural people in this country face, particularly the grain growing ones which are in such dire straits, is precisely because of the United States' deliberate violation of that supposedly friendly agreement between themselves and Canada. They have used an export enhancement program to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars to steal from the Canadian agricultural producers traditional markets. As a

result, our ability to sell grain abroad has certainly been reduced, to the detriment of our agricultural producers.
The North American free trade agreement, signed already, hopefully will never be implemented. Certainly as a New Democrat I can assure you that we will be doing everything we can to make sure that it is never implemented. In reference to some of the things involved in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade our government is saying: "Well, it's okay, folks, we will go to tariffication if we lose the ability to have our marketing boards in Canada. Marketing boards are really our first stand but we can always fall back to tariffication and then the farmers will be protected that way. We can put tariffs in place to protect the farmers on that". Generally the reference is to the tariff protocol referred to in the free trade agreement with the United States but not referred to at all in the NAFTA. There is specifically an exclusion of any kind of tariff protocol for agricultural products within the North America free trade agreement.
With reference to the wheat board, which is such an absolutely essential institution brought in by a Conservative government during the days of the Depression, absolutely essential to the farmer in getting a fair return for his products on the prairies, this government has done almost everything it can to gut the wheat board. It has removed oats from the wheat board to the detriment of the price of oats.
I see that I have only a minute left. Let me just say that the experience is that with the removal of oats from the wheat board, the price has suffered. Now barley is going to be removed from the protection of the wheat board. We can certainly conclude that the same will happen there. Organization after organization after organization is saying please, do not do it, begging the minister responsible for the wheat board not to do that, after him having said that the best thing he ever did was to remove oats from the wheat board. Well, no more favours from the minister; please leave the wheat board alone and put it back to its former glory.
There are many more things I could refer to. Poverty in Saskatoon, the city I come from, is the second worst in the country behind Manitoba. For heaven's sake, we are behind Newfoundland which for so long had been considered to be an impoverished province. That is what the legacy of this government has been to this nation and my constituency.
Yes, the people have been calling for an election. Please call an election and relieve us of this torture.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague from the prairie province of Saskatchewan has spoken and has ended with great eloquence.
It is an eloquence that can only be repeated by the constant plea of my own constituents in the great city of Toronto. I would have said that magnificent city of Toronto, but unfortunately we have had to use more humble adjectives over the course of the last several years, in large measure and in fact almost completely thanks to the government opposite.
The city of Toronto is that great engine that drove much of the economy of Ontario and contributed in its munificence through taxes and revenues to the greater glory of all Canadian industry and social programs. I do not speak with any blushing for the constituents of Toronto who have done that so willingly as Canadians.
They find themselves today, thanks to the government opposite, with an unemployment rate that has seen close to a quarter of a million Canadians from the Ibronto area on the unemployment rolls. Think about that. There is the winging of 250,000 people. My colleagues opposite might do a little geographical research very quickly to see how many cities in Canada number 250,000 people. There are 250,000 unemployed in that place in Canada that used to drive the economic engine of the nation.
That is drastic. So tragic is the outcome of the government's economic policies in its tenure in office that even the banks, the great bastion of profitability, have taken to laying people off. The economic financial centre of Canada is close to being no more. My colleagues opposite are suggesting that perhaps we should be serious on this side of the House while they go about their business of cutting the deficit, reducing government operations and employing other types of techniques which remain a mystery in the way they will function to all Canadians but those who sit opposite on that side of the House.
February 2, 1993

I have with me my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood who has presented on many occasions suggestions for tax policy, economic policy, industrial development or assistance to the entrepreneurs who used to highlight the character of Canada that was symbolized by its innovation, its risk-taking desire and its willingness to take that extra challenge in order to produce wealth to be shared by all Canadians.
A few moments ago, my colleague could not help but wonder where the ideas that should have emerged from the administration offices have gone. They probably went the way of our trade balance. Over the course of the eight years of this administration, we have gone from a trade balance of $19.8 billion to a mere $7.4 billion.
This is from a nation whose dependency on international trade is recognized by each and every one of us. This is by a government that says that close to 35 cents out of every Canadian dollar earned is earned from international trade. This is from a government that says that the future lies with the growth of international trade. It says this while it increases the dependence of Canadian goods on one client. Imagine what would happen to anybody running a business and counts on 80 cents for every dollar earned on one client alone. What shoddy planning. What absolutely abysmal near-sightedness. Just this week on an international platform in an international environment in Davos, Switzerland we see that our trade people are bereft of any representation by senior members of government. They are getting snookered by the Mexicans who are part of the North American free trade agreement.
Mexicans are in Europe looking for and pursuing new clients for products that are going to be coming out of North America. They are looking for new investment and new investors and are trying to create opportunities. Where is our government?
Where are others?

Try not to defend the government by asking where are others? Take a look at what has happened. It is nowhere to be seen. In the richest market in the entire
Government Orders
world it is nowhere to be see. It is content to continue to reduce Canada to an exporter of resources only and to one client. Is it any wonder then that over the course of the administration of the government opposite our current account balance has gone from a suqtlus of $3.4 billion in 1984 to a deficit of $24.7 billion just this last year? Shame. That is an absolutely horrid shame.
This is a government that came into power with the stated desire to create jobs, to cut taxes, and to create a better environment for Canadians. It says it is trying to create wealth for Canadians. What did it do? Since 1984 direct income taxes have gone up from $37.5 billion to $73.5 billion just a year and a half ago.
Corporate taxes have actually decreased over that same period of time. They have decreased from $11.3 billion to $10.8 billion. This is a government that does not understand how to use tax policy to create wealth. It does not do anything for trade. It does not do anything for planning. Planning is a misnomer for anything that it has done with respect to the GST.
The government initially planned on gamisheeing in the range of $25.5 billion to $28 billion with a 7 per cent tax based on an exchange of goods and services of approximately $400 billion. That was the value of that exchange. That should have brought to our treasury approximately $28 billion.
Last year the government was able, or at least this is what it reports, to collect $15.5 billion. Either it has succeeded in driving 50 per cent of the market underground, and experts admit that the minimum that has been driven underground is 15 per cent, or its estimates were wrong all along, or, and I hate to say it, it is deliberately deceiving everybody with the figures it is putting out. Right now on the basis of revenues collected so far this year it is again another $1.3 billion short.
This is a government that has used taxes to whip Canadians into submission. Since 1984 indirect taxes have increased from $18.12 billion to $28.57 billion. When it is taking this kind of money from the marketplace, from Canadians, what is it forcing them to do? We have seen some of them go underground. Others have moved south. Enterprise has diminished and risk-taking has been discouraged. Even worse it has also forced municipalities and provinces to assume the burden that exists among the general electorate.

Government Orders
I see that some of the members opposite have difficulty dealing with the reality of the statistics that come from their own department. Perhaps this is yet another indication that they are not only tired but insensitive and, dare I say it, unable to read the signs. They should leave and leave today.

Mr. Speaker, as I was looking over the statistics that I received from my colleague from Eglinton-Lawrence I could not help but wonder how the government could possibly think it could get away with these incredible tax increases.
In 1984 the federal revenue from income tax was $37.5 billion. In 1990 it was $73 billion, and that figure does include inflation. As well in 1990 there was close to $15 billion in GST revenues. That money came out of the system and came from individuals. Therefore, we are talking about a comparison of about $37 billion in 1984 to almost $90 billion in 1990, if we include the GST.
That is one of the reasons there is very little confidence or spirit in this country right now. I do not want to ignore the reality of there being absolutely no inflation in this country. However the ratchet the government has used on inflation has been too aggressive. It is nice to talk about there being absolutely no inflation in this country. Yesterday the Prime Minister said in the House that we have the lowest inflation in 30 years. However he must recognize that there must be a balance. When there are so many people on unemployment and welfare Canadians would rather have a little more inflation and have people in the work force with the dignity of a job.
The same goes for interest rates. We could say because of the lower inflation that we have the lowest annualized interest rates in 20 years. I recognize that. However the problem is that there is no confidence. There is no will to move ahead. Surely the government is not stupid. There are intelligent people over there. They are hearing the same things that we are hearing. How long are they going to let this torture continue? It must drive them as crazy as it is driving us. It must be the same torture for them as it is for us. What are they waiting for?
There are ways of igniting the entrepreneurial spirit in this countiy. I want to mention the Small Businesses Loans Act which the Minister of Finance presented in his financial address before Christmas. The Small Businesses Loans Act is a good piece of legislation. There are areas for improvement in it. The $5 million ceiling for eligibility is a little low. The fact that we have an instrument that will force the financial institutions of this country to loan money to small businesses, and that 85 per cent of the loan is guaranteed by the Crown, is a good thing.
I am hearing two things from the small businesses in my riding.
First, I am hearing that most of the bank managers are not aware of it or do not want to get involved in the paper work. The government must use its force and influence to force the financial institutions of this country to implement this piece of legislation. We give the financial institutions of this country all kinds of tax preferences and legal loopholes. We are hearing from these bank managers right now. The president of the Bank of Montreal says that he has ways to ignite the economy. Let us challenge him.
How many small business loans has he given out under the Small Businesses Loans Act? Why does the government not use its influence to bring these banks to a state of accountability? I read a speech the other day by the president of the Royal Bank in which he said that small business entrepreneurship is where it is at in terms of getting people back to work.
I say this in a constructive way. Why do we not take the Small Businesses Loans Act, a piece of legislation that all of us in this House support, and force these bankers to use it. The greatest hope of new job creation lies with the small businessmen and women of this country, with people who want to have a home-based business. Today with the new technology and the new economy people can start businesses right from their own recreation rooms or homes. However, they need access to capital. We have an instrument in this House but we are not using it.
The government cannot say that what I am saying is not constructive. It is totally constructive. However the government is not acting.
It is really sad to hear the glib comments over there when there are so many people who are having a tough time making it from payroll to payroll. There are so many people out there right now who are in such pain, who are in real pain. What are we doing here? Are we

Mr. Speaker, the members of this House are using this debate to put on record some of their thoughts on the government's economic policy and on the course of action we in this country should be taking to try to achieve full employment and to get the economy of this country back on track.
I would like to join in that effort and to discuss with the members of this House some ideas that I think should be looked at by the people of Canada if we are going to get our economy right.
Government Orders
Here is the first question. What is the goal of government economic policy? Over the last eight years, and particularly with the dominance of John Crow as the Governor of the Bank of Canada, this government has focused on the objective of reducing inflation to zero. The Governor of the Bank of Canada, along with the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, has made much of the gains they have made in reducing inflation to zero. They have placed this goal ahead of the goal of achieving full employment and keeping Canadians working and expanding the base of work across this country.
The result of these policies, of course, has been disastrous for Canadians. What we we hear from the government is that they are now bereft of new ideas. They continue to persist in the assumption that the free trade agreement and NAFTA have been good for Canada when in fact it is evident to every Canadian that the free trade agreement has failed and has caused miserable unemployment. This is particularly so in central Canada. It has deprived our legislatures right across this country of the capacity to deal with the economic problems we face.
The government has added to the deficit, rather than decreased it, as the natural result of its policies. If one reduces economic activity, which has been the government's set purpose, government revenues decline. If you do that through the device of high interest rates, the government cost of borrowing increases. Therefore, we have had the phenomenon of this Conservative government, and other Conservative governments across Canada, running higher and higher deficits. Year after year these people come back to Parliament or to the legislatures to explain. "Oh my goodness, we're sorry, we were out of line last year. We underestimated the deficit. The deficit has actually increased when we meant to decrease it".
Caught in this desperate mix, these governments continue to follow the same policies. They continue to cut back on public investment. They continue to scare private investment out of the market. They continue to keep interests higher than they should be. They continue, therefore, to add to the deficit rather than detract from it. They are caught in the spiral and Canadians are caught in the spiral with them.
Let me suggest that there are alternative economic policies that the people of Canada should be considering and that this Parliament should consider. First, we must get our goals right. The goal of an economic policy for our country should be to encourage employment for its people. That must be the objective and it must be the prime and overriding objective. It is through employ-

Government Orders
ment that people participate in society. I see it as a moral and ethical obligation on government to provide the opportunity for work for all its people. I believe other governments have demonstrated that it is possible to do so. If we had a government that would co-operate with provincial governments-rather than fight with them- perhaps we could pull together in this country to achieve the objective of full employment for our people.
Specifically, I would suggest the following. First, we need tax policies which focus on getting private capital investment moving again, particularly in small and local businesses.
Second, government financial priorities must focus on job creation. All government expenditures should be judged on that basis. We need to encourage public investment rather than discourage it. We must be encouraging the development of social programs which in turn provide jobs for people. We must be encouraging rather than discouraging the arts, culture and heritage because these are job creators in themselves.
Government financial policies should not focus on cutbacks, but should focus on maintaining employment in the public sector and in related sectors.
Third, the government must move to reduce interest rates even further. The Canadian public will be seeing interest rates that are lower than they have been but the public must also understand that our interest rates still remain substantially higher than they should be when related to the rate of inflation. There is significant room to further reduce interest rates in this country.
Fourth, the government must be prepared to allow the Canadian dollar to fall further. There has been a drop over the last period but it should fall significantly further. We are an export economy. We depend on tourism exports for our livelihood. This will stimulate and help our economy.
Fifth, we should encourage Canadian investment. It is critically important that we begin to regain control of our economy. Under this government, more and more of our economy has continued to be owned by outsiders. It is important that we begin to change the direction of investment so that Canadians increasingly can regain control of their own economy.
This of course applies to trade policies, which is the sixth point. Clearly the government's trade policies have failed. It is essential that we should cancel the free trade agreement, that we should not proceed with NAFTA and that we should develop a totally different set of trading relations with our partners than this government and its Liberal friends have agreed to.
Seventh, we must put a real emphasis on training and education. Training and education are at the heart of where we are as a country. We have one of the worst over-all records in terms of training and education policies of all industrial countries. We spend more and receive less. We do so because the central government, the federal government, has failed in its role of pulling together all of those involved. It is not just provincial governments but school boards and local governments, universities, colleges, the private education sector, business and labour across this country that are needed to develop a unified education and training policy in this country.
Let me give the government credit in the area of the competitiveness study or the prosperity initiative. The educational side of that study produced a number of significant ideas and it is time this government acted on those ideas.
Eighth, we need community-based economic planning. We had an economic workshop in my riding. I convened people from every sector of the community. We sat for a day and looked at ways in which the federal government can encourage job creation in Victoria. This workshop came up with a number of very good specific ideas: an ocean engineering centre, a community learning council, heritage arts and culture policies which would be of assistance, regional economic planning and a harbour that can be at the heart of job creation in Victoria. These are ideas which do not depend on substantial federal government largess, but do depend on government being ready to encourage local initiative and community ideas.
Ninth, it should reduce the deficit on a step-by-step basis rather than attempting to do it overnight when, as I showed earlier, that produces the opposite reaction.
February 2, 1993

Tenth, there should be a willingness to accept a moderate rate of inflation. It is clear that a zero rate of inflation is bad for the economy. Our economy, as has been shown since the end of the Second World War, functions most effectively with a moderate rate of inflation.
What is that?
It is inflation of two, three or four per cent, in that order.
How about one per cent to one and a half per cent?

My friend says one per cent to one and a half per cent, but he knows that that in fact for most people is effectively zero or minus zero inflation. We have an economic policy. It is important that this country proceeds with it. We can achieve full employment under these policies.

He engaged in a creative rewriting of the economic history of Ontario in an effort to show that the New Democratic Party somehow was not responsible for the huge debt that the province of Ontario is now encumbered with thanks to Mr. Rae's government. The Minister of Supply and Services was here and heard this balderdash this morning when it was suggested, apparently quite seriously, that the reason there is a $10 billion deficit in Ontario today is because

the NDP inherited a $3 billion deficit when they took over from the Liberals in 1990.
Of course we know that in 1990 the recession began. Certainly economic projections both in Ontario and nationally changed as a result of the recession that began in that year. The campaign in Ontario was conducted during August. By September it was apparent that what had been projected to be a surplus in the accounts of the province of Ontario for the financial year ending in March 1991 was rapidly deteriorating and turning into a deficit.
The new government increased the deficit by fiddling the books. It changed accounting practices part way through the year to include in the 1991-92 year certain figures that would not normally have been included. It took the view that it might as well get the deficit up so it would not look quite so bad the next year. It also had a pot or a contingency fund that was allowed for in the estimates. That had not been spent when it took office in September 1990 and it promptly spent that money.
The Ontario NDP government increased the deficit by about $1.5 billion from what it otherwise would have been-in effect doubling it that one year-and claimed that that was the Liberal deficit. It was not. The NDP took over responsibility halfway through the year. It ran up the costs by fiddling the books and charging this extra money to the accounts. Then it said: "We inherited a $3 billion debt". Then the hon. member for Essex-Windsor, with a straight face, said it set to work to fix up that mess but somehow managed to increase the deficit from $3 billion to $10 billion in one year, and that was after its own budget. It introduced a budget supposedly to fix the problem and it fixed it all right. It tripled the deficit in one year.

Mr. Speaker, it is true there have been a large number of bankruptcies in Canada this year. Some of them are due to the slow-down of the economy and some are due to the adjustment, the restructuring and rationalization that is taking place in the Canadian economy.
I remind the hon. member that the figures for December show that bankruptcies fell to the lowest level in four months, the lowest level since August. Obviously there is a turn around and some of the effects of the policies of the Government of Canada, the adjustment that is taking place, the restructuring that is taking place are starting to settle in.
The fundamentals are in place. It is noted that today the interest rates fell further. That is encouraging news. As I indicated, there has been new job creation in seven of the last eight months. We have had growth in the last six consecutive quarters. Therefore there are some positive indicators.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a bit amusing because on February 4, 1992 the minister said there was a decline in December of the previous year. Using the same argument, he concluded that it would be better in 1992.
He is serving us the same argument that did not work last year. There was an increase last year over the previous year. Another promise the government cannot keep is a reduction in the number of bankruptcies in Canada.

I would like to put a question to the Minister of Finance because this morning he asked Canadians to give him suggestions for a budget that should normally be presented in the month of February and has now been postponed indefinitely, for all we know.
I would like to tell the Minister of Finance that we suggested to him over a year ago that an infrastructure program be created in conjunction with provincial and municipal governments. This would result in immediate job creation and produce infrastructures that would be useful to all Canadians in the years to come.
Why does the Minister of Finance refuse to accept our suggestion? Is it because it comes from the opposition?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that suggestion made from time to time by the hon. member has been discarded because quite frankly, he has not been able to outline to the Canadian people and to the House where the money would come from.
February 2, 1993

He said billions of dollars would be spent by the federal government, the provincial government and the municipal government. All of that money would have to be borrowed or raised in the form of taxation. He has not fulfilled his undertaking to explain just how that would be financed.
Speaking of suggestions, I am rather enamoured with the suggestion the hon. member made yesterday. As a substitute for the GST, he is talking about a hidden, secretive and sneaky tax which would tax food and would be buried so that Canadians would not know how he was going to tax the Canadian people. What a sham. We are not going to buy that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have always said that when there is a program that the municipalities are asking for, they have their financial problems, but they believe that to have an economy that works we need growth. There are 1.7 million people unemployed and the country wants growth. When will the minister stop fighting inflation? The economic policies of his government are completely bankrupt. That is why we have statistics on that today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is interesting how the hon. member evades the veiy salient issue which has been raised. I asked the hon. Leader of the Opposition to come-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Call an election, chicken.
That is what you said in 1991.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Are they ever sensitive over there. Are they ever sensitive about this issue. I asked very simply that the hon. Leader of the Opposition come clean. Is he proposing a hidden form of secretive, sneaky tax to replace the GST? Is he proposing a tax that would tax food? Yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Twelve months ago the minister when faced with record bankruptcies had a choice: change his economic policies or do nothing. He chose the latter. The result is
77,000	additional economic casualties of this government's fiscal policies.
Was it just plain incompetence or typical Tory arrogance that allowed the Minister of Finance to sit and do
Oral Questions
nothing while 77,000 Canadians were pushed beyond the brink into bankruptcy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my December statement outlining an economic plan there are clearly a number of very positive initiatives that will bolster growth, that will create jobs, that will generate economic activity particularly in the small business sector.
There are a number of initiatives that will beef up the small business sector and encourage the growth of jobs and strengthen and enhance that very important job creation sector.
It is interesting to note that the Liberals opposite oppose any solid initiative. What they want to do is tax and spend and borrow. That is not our policy.

Mr. Speaker, let us talk about the business climate in Canada for a minute. In the minister's own province of Alberta business bankruptcies are up by 12 per cent. In the province of Ontario they are up by 16 per cent. In the province of Nova Scotia they are up by 25 per cent. That is this government's record of inaction in dealing with the business community in Canada.
How can the Minister of Finance feel anything but shame with the fact that under his direction and stewardship thousands of Canadians, 77,000 Canadians, have been driven belly up into bankruptcy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated there have been a number of business casualties. I have not ignored that fact. I also indicated, and it is fair to acknowledge, that bankruptcies in the month of December fell to their lowest level in four months.
The hon. member asks me what we are doing. Well, if he would just listen for a few minutes, last December we announced initiatives that froze UI premiums to provide a premium holiday for new employees. There is the 10 per cent investment tax credit for new purchases of machinery so that businesses can become more competitive and more productive. We have improved access to capital, announced improvements to R and D, improvements in the treatment of capital cost allowances and high-tech equipment, renewed funding for the IRAP, announced an extension of the home buyers plan and provided assistance for the oil and gas sector and assistance for the mining sector.

February 2, 1993
Oral Questions
Those are all positive initiatives that are now starting to have a pay-off for Canadians and for the economic activity and particularly for the jobless.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
The minister has said that his policies are a great success. Today we have just learned that the number of bankruptcies last year broke all Canadian records. This government's policies are a total failure.
Yesterday the Prime Minister asked for alternatives and suggestions. I have a suggestion for the Minister of Finance: eliminate the tax shelters, created by the Liberal government, for rich people family trusts. This is a good suggestion.
It was unjust then, and it still is. Why does the government not close this loophole and use the money to create jobs and save small businesses?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is precisely what we are doing. We are closing the loopholes so that these trust beneficiaries will not evade capital gains tax.
This government's record in terms of closing the so-called Liberal loopholes is very dramatic in fashion. I would be glad to document it and send the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party an itemized list of every initiative we took which closes the loopholes left by the previous administration.

Mr. Speaker, the reality is that this government has closed more factories than it has closed tax loopholes and has lost more jobs than it has created.
There are many things the Minister of Finance could do. Ele could close the private family trusts for the wealthy. He could close that tax loophole as well as the business entertainment expenses deduction, the capital gains exemptions for the wealthy and the interest deductibility for offshore companies.
I say to the Minister of Finance that if he wants to get revenue to support the creation of jobs and the future of Canadians, why does he not close these loopholes? Why does he not do it now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party is suggesting is that she would like to make it more difficult for the small business sector to do business in this country. We do not subscribe to that.
With respect to trusts, I ask her to read the legislation again. She will find that the loophole is being closed.
I could name 20 different items that we have addressed. We ended the abuse of the scientific research tax credit. We eliminated tax shelters based on investments in yachts, recreation vehicles and similar projects. We halted income splitting. We stopped the so-called carve-out transaction.

Mr. Speaker, it is always amazing that the great successes that are listed just create more devastation for Canadians. So I will make another suggestion to the Minister of Finance.
In a positive vein and with good intent I want to say to the minister that independent analysts have said the elimination of the GST could create over 300,000 jobs in Canada. Unlike my hon. colleague, the Leader of the Opposition, I am prepared to talk about alternatives before the election, not after. Clearly the elimination of the GST would create jobs in Canada. Why will the minister not look at this option?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party is really stretching her credibility. What would she substitute it with? It generates some $15 billion to $16 billion.
We know what the Liberals want. They want a hidden, secretive and sneaky tax. What does the NDP want? She will have to come clean and tell us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. In the November 1992 report to the House of Commons, the Auditor General reported that the defence program management system was, to use his term, expensive and ineffective.
February 2, 1993

Considering the magnitude of major projects involved, about $3 billion a year, this is a very serious indictment.
I would like to ask the Minister of National Defence what action she has planned either to refute this serious claim or to take immediate corrective actions.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of my briefings at the Department of National Defence, I have been very interested in the question of fiscal management throughout the department.
It is important to assure Canadians, simply because of the magnitude of the budget of the Department of National Defence, it is a department that is managed to the highest standards possible. I would be very pleased to discuss with the hon. member any approaches which he may have.
I am looking carefully at the Auditor General's report and I hope to be able to report further on this subject to the House of Commons as initiatives develop.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question for the minister. While it is not just my concern, it is the concern of the Auditor General and I would be happy to talk with her at any time at all.
I would like to get more specific now. One of the specific concerns of the Auditor General was that most of the problems observed with the major capital programs were generated in the project life cycle, early in the project initiation or in the very early stages of the project. He went on to say that none of the projects examined were directly related to defence policy and that most of the equipment failed to meet the operational requirements. That is what the Auditor General said.
Given the seriousness of this claim and the fact that the program we are looking at now is going to be one of the largest in Canada and probably one of the largest ever in DND, second or third anyway, could the minister tell this House how this charge of the Auditor General applies to the Sea King replacement program or more specifically to the $4.5 billion EH-101 helicopter program.
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. As do many Canadians, he knows of the tragic situation at Davis Inlet, Labrador.
I want to ask the minister today what is his response to the cry for help that has come from Davis Inlet. What does he intend to do immediately, both for the short term and the long term, to respond to that community and particularly to the children whose lives are threatened?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of this House, indeed all Canadians are saddened and deeply troubled by the spectre of young children resorting to gasoline sniffing and substance abuse and the unacceptable conditions in Davis Inlet in which they and their parents are living.
I have discussed this matter extensively with my colleagues, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans from Newfoundland and Labrador. Yesterday I called the acting premier, Mr. Winston Baker, in Mr. Wells' absence about what the two governments collectively might do to deal with the immediate problem of the human condition in Davis Inlet.

Oral Questions
It is important for members of the House to recognize that the community, which was established some 25 years ago, is totally inadequate for the present population. It is some four times larger now than the infrastructure which was designed when the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador moved those people there a quarter of a century ago.
We have contemplated the relocation of the community to another location on the mainland. A consultant's report received on December 18 recommends that the government seriously consider that option. That is a long-term solution.
If we bear in mind that the previous relocation 25 years ago has led to the present circumstances, relocation in itself is not the solution to the problem.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare is in Halifax today meeting officials and will in all likelihood meet Innu representatives tomorrow while he is there. Officials of both governments-
Time.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the House wanted an extensive report on this very serious question.
I will conclude by saying this. Representatives of both governments have invited the Innu to sit down later this week and among options decide what to do about the immediate problem of substance abuse and inadequate conditions in that community.

Mr. Speaker, the immediate problem is substance abuse.
I would like to ask the minister a very specific question, a question I think the people of Davis Inlet would ask if they were here today. Can they have their own treatment centre and their own treatment program near Davis Inlet, culturally based and in their own language? This is what the people want. I ask the minister today if he is in a position to respond to that serious and important request from the people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I spoke to the Minister of National Health and Welfare this morning. I am assured he will be making a statement on this matter before this time tomorrow.
I should also point out that these children are wards of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador which has clear legal jurisdiction for health care and welfare. Any decision on whether they are to be removed from the present community either to a near location or a centre
further away will be taken in consultation with the Innu leadership and with the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
The social disintegration of the Innu community at Davis Inlet dates to its forced relocation to a remote island in 1967 by the Government of Newfoundland, assisted by a local priest. Those people were cut off from their traditional way of life and subsistence, left without promised housing or running water and abandoned by the federal government which knew it had the constitutional responsibility for them.
Why has the federal government refused to acknowledge its constitutional responsibility for aboriginal people in Newfoundland when its own legal opinions from the Department of Justice have confirmed this responsibility since 1950?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, later today we will be releasing a full statement and account of the background to this tragic situation.
I remind the hon. member that he should read the history because if he did he would discover that the community of old Davis Inlet which existed prior to 1950 was but three miles from the present community of new Davis Inlet. There was another relocation north in the late 1940s which failed. It is a fact that on the island where both the old Davis Inlet and the modem community are located, there is an inadequate supply of wildlife and natural resources to support the people who live there.
From the time of Confederation, Newfoundland has accepted legal and jurisdictional responsibility for the Innu people who are not registered and not status Indian people. Therefore they are not entitled to the benefits of my department directly and have chosen to remain as not registered, non-status Indian people under the care of the province of Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, on February 19 last year I asked the minister to relocate the Davis Inlet Innu. Since my question the federal and provincial governments and the Innu themselves have all studied relocation and found that relocation to the mainland is the best and cheapest option for this community.
February 2, 1993

When will the government finally accept its legal and moral responsibility, commit the necessary funds and begin the process of moving the Davis Inlet people to a new community on the Labrador mainland?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might repeat what I said to the hon. member for Labrador a moment ago. We would not want to repeat the mistake that has already been made. That is why an extensive consultant's study was undertaken at my request. It found that a relocation could be desirable but might not solve the human and social problems that exist in that community.
Therefore, in consultation with the Inuit leadership and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador which has legal responsibility for the care and well-being of these people, we will find an appropriate solution.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade.
On Friday the Prime Minister is visiting President Clinton in Washington. Presumably the current steel dispute will be discussed between them. Could the minister tell the House whether the Prime Minister will take the view, as the minister said yesterday the problem lies with the Industry in Canada, that it is a management and labour problem".
Will the Prime Minister protect and defend Canadian interests by seeking a continent-wide steel pact or, more fundamentally, seek negotiation of what is a subsidy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I was doing yesterday was correcting a distortion that the hon. member for Hamilton East had put on the record. She was blaming the total problems of the steel industry on the fact that it got hit with the anti-dumping duties last week.
The point I was making is that there is a significant reduction in the competitive advantage of the steel
Oral Questions
industry amounting to $100 a tonne or 20 per cent of the value of the product. That is the problem.
On the question that my hon. friend puts, yes, I propose as I have already done, to raise the question of a Canada-U.S. steel pact with the Americans. The Prime Minister has already done that with the previous president and I presume he will be doing the same thing this week.
Our approach is to establish a blue ribbon panel to develop the framework for such an agreement and then see whether we can negotiate an agreement at a later stage.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows that a U.S.-Canada steel pact, like the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement or the North American free trade agreement, would be essentially flawed unless there is an agreement on what is a subsidy, unless there is an anti-dumping code. That is the void in the free trade agreement. That is the black hole in the North American free trade agreement.
Will the minister tell the House not about a blue ribbon commission but when this government is going to address that fundamental question with the United States and now with Mexico of what is a subsidy and how we can achieve an anti-dumping code. Then the problems in the steel industry will be finally resolved.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is precisely what is being addressed in the Uruguay round of negotiations in Geneva.
If my hon. friend will review what has been decided to date on the definition of a subsidy and how the anti-subsidy disputes can be settled, he will see that there has been significant progress.
On the question of anti-dumping, my hon. friend is quite right. The United States has been absolutely adamant. Even in the Uruguay round, with a large bulk of countries trying to encourage the United States to change its anti-dumping regime, there has been no support for that within the U.S. industry or the U.S. Congress. We continue to press the Americans and I appreciate the support of the hon. member in that direction.

February 2, 1993
Oral Questions
It is difficult to move the United States even in the multilateral negotiations with so many other countries on our side.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture.
The minister knows that farm income is expected to drop about a billion dollars this year. That is a drop of about 21 per cent. Today we learned that bankruptcies in agriculture and related service industries reached 421 last year.
The situation for thousands of producers is desperate and that explains partly why over 13,000 farmers attended a rally in Saskatoon last week.
What does the minister plan to do to help farmers stay on the land and maintain rural life?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not all bad news. The hon. member will know that the Canadian Wheat Board just raised the additional payment for barley and he will know that we reached an agreement with Saskatchewan about two weeks ago that will see additional money flow into Saskatchewan. In total he will see some $260 million additional flow into farm safety net programs this year.
He will know that even though prices are not expected to improve very much, there are good prospects for grain sales and over all on a net basis government programs, federal and provincial, will put over $2 billion into farmers' hands this calendar year.
What we intend to do is work very hard at all levels of government, especially as the Prime Minister has done in the past, to see what we can do about improving international grain prices.
To say again, while there are and will continue to be concerns until we reach some agreements on international trade, the news is not necessarily all bad as far as income is concerned for farmers for the coming year.

Mr. Speaker, I want to pick up on that aid package that was negotiated for Saskatchewan. There is only about 20 million new dollars of federal money in that aid package.
While farmers are grateful for anything they get, it should also be noted at the same time that under the WGTA freight assistance has been cut by this government this year to the tune of $70 million. It is give with one hand and take away with the other. That kind of hypocrisy underlines the agricultural policy of this government.
Again I ask the Minister of Agriculture what his government intends to do to keep farmers on the land and maintain rural life.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again, the hon. member cannot have it both ways. We have done considerable to control over-all government expenditures that sees a reduction in interest rates to farmers. He should know that every percentage point reduction in interest rates for farmers literally means hundreds of millions of dollars of saved expenses.
He will also know that in some areas farm input costs have not gone up and in some cases they have gone down. There are five chemicals that will be less in price this spring than they were last year.
Again, it is not an easy situation to address. We are putting out a considerable amount of support. He will know that in the economic statement of last December one of the three areas that the Minister of Finance did not touch was an over-all reduction in safety net programs. They stayed the way they were.
You can take from that that the government is veiy committed to doing what it can to support farmers through a very difficult time.

February 2, 1993

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Justice. The Canadian justice system is failing to protect women from former boyfriends and husbands who follow, harass and threaten them.
In three recent murder cases in Manitoba and in others across the country, the murderers were actually in possession of restraining orders telling them to stay away from the victims. In at least two of these cases the system failed to take away firearms which were in the possession of the murderers. These firearms were actually used in the killings.
When is the minister going to do something? Why will he not bring forward changes to the Criminal Code to protect these women from this harm?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Justice, Attorney General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that my colleague raises a rather important point. Indeed, the Criminal Code has provisions in sections 177, 264, 372 and 423 that allow police officers and the courts to intervene.
I realize that the administration of justice is left to the provincial governments. It is therefore important for us to make sure that we know the reasons behind this system and the sections of the Criminal Code that may apply in some cases like the one he just mentioned. Unfortunately, such incidents happen.
I said yesterday, and I repeat today, that our government intends to act quickly on that. We are now reviewing those sections of the Criminal Code and if necessary, we will act quickly to bring legislation on it to the House.

Mr. Speaker, the police say that they cannot do anything until the victim is harmed. These who are being stalked are living in terror.
Just assuming that the provisions were in the Criminal Code now, which certainly not everyone agrees with, how is the Minister of Justice going to force all the attorneys general in Canada to do something.
Why does the Minister of Justice not just amend the law so there is no question, and the lives of more women in this country are not risked? Will he bring forward these amendments immediately, certainly before a prorogation of this House?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Justice, Attorney General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to enter into this debate today.
I want to refer to some areas that are not always discussed in this House. That is mainly the areas concerning agriculture and in a broader sense, rural Canada.
We spend approximately a billion dollars on agriculture every year. In the last eight or nine years, something like $16 billion has been given in direct payments to agriculture. Although huge sums have been paid out, the fact is that in Saskatchewan alone some 1,500 farmers are leaving the land every year and similar numbers are quitting in other provinces.
The question that has to be answered is this. In what direction are we heading with respect to agriculture in this country? The government has not given any clear direction other than it is willing to spend money on agriculture, usually at times when it is convenient for the government to help members get re-elected or when it is going to help an agribusiness that is going to remove farm families from the land and destroy rural communities.
This government does not understand, does not have an appreciation of what is happening at this time. This was made abundantly clear yesterday when I asked the Prime Minister about the problems in agriculture. I want to quote from Hansard of yesterday when the Prime Minister in his response to my question stated:
This government brought in the GRIP program. This government
brought in the NISA program. Both programs are greatly admired
by Saskatchewan fanners.
I do not know of anyone in Saskatchewan or in this country who admires the GRIP. The answer shows a complete lack of understanding, a complete ignorance in this area. I do not blame the Prime Minister. He is obviously getting bad advice from his new Minister of Agriculture.
February 2, 1993

Up until the last cabinet shuffle we had three Ministers of Agriculture. What happened after that last shuffle? We lost one outright. The Minister of State for Agriculture, who is concerned with agriculture in Quebec, is now the Minister of Justice. I doubt very much whether that minister is going to be spending very much time on agriculture. He is going to be spending more time on justice. It is a major portfolio in itself. There are many areas of agriculture that have to be dealt with. Therefore, we are left with one Minister of Agriculture.
I would suggest this government is taking a new direction. It is abandoning the concerns it has with agriculture. To leave one member as a Minister of Agriculture, with all the needs and requirements there are in this area, certainly does not bode well for the future of agriculture in this country.
The Prime Minister went on to state in response to my question:
I would like to tell my hon. friend this. This government increased
aid to agriculture including western agriculture, over the eight year
period by 650 per cent.
That is also true. However, the way money was spent on agriculture, farmers should be upset, rural people should be upset, urban people should be upset, Canadian taxpayers should be upset because money was wasted. Billions and billions of dollars were wasted. Yet the Prime Minister can say that farmers in Saskatchewan adore NISA, they adore GRIP. Patently that is not the case.
What is needed is not spending more money on agriculture, it is to spend money more wisely on agriculture. The GRIP we have today is like putting a farmer on a step ladder with a noose around his neck and every year forcing him one step down the ladder. It is slowly going to destroy the family farm. When we have a program that gives some farmers a GRIP cheque big enough to buy a half section of land and other fanners a GRIP cheque that will not even pay their fuel bills, there is something wrong with that program.
We in this party have been saying that what we have to do is first of all state our objective clearly. That objective is that we want to maintain viable farm families, viable rural communities in this country. This is not going to be accomplished with the set of programs which the government opposite has been promoting. It was made very clear last week when over 13,000 people came to Saskatoon. They were not all farmers, some were from urban
Government Orders
areas; they were not all from Saskatchewan, there were some from Alberta and some from Manitoba. They made it very clear that they did not like GRIP, whether it was Saskatchewan GRIP or Alberta GRIP or Manitoba GRIP. It made no difference. The fact is that the agriculture programs that are in place now are not the ones that we require.
The Prime Minister yesterday gave me, with all due respect, a glib answer, an answer that people in this country who have any knowledge of agriculture would mock. It is unfortunate that this is apparently the advice he gets from his Minister of Agriculture.
We have to pursue three underlying points with respect to agriculture and rural Canada generally. First, we have to realize that the primary resource sector in this country, the key sector, depends on maintaining rural Canada, whether that sector is agriculture, whether it is the fisheries, whether it is forestry or whether it is mining in those regions of Canada where there is mining.
This government has not recognized that fact. We have seen the destruction of the fishing industry off the Newfoundland coast, which is wreaking havoc in Newfoundland. We heard the remark made by the Prime Minister showing a complete lack of knowledge of what is happening in western Canada.
Until we recognize that the primary resource sector is the key sector, there is going to be problems and the government is going to be called upon to make emergency payments and come up with money to help people in those areas. Agricultural policies have to be developed with a view to maintaining those communities and maintaining farm families.
If somebody wants to farm 10 or 12 or 15 sections of land, go ahead and farm it but do not expect the government to help you keep that land and buy out other farms. We want programs that will spend money wisely. We do not have a lot of money to spend in this country and we spend far more than we should right now with the deficit we have. The money we spend now on agriculture could be spent in a much better way, where it would produce much better results and provide a much stronger infrastructure if we recognize that the primary resource sector is the key to rural Canada, and if we develop a program with a view to maintaining rural communities and farm families in western Canada.

Government Orders
Another thing we need is the co-ordination of programs. We have the Community Futures Program which is under the Department of Employment and Immigration. We also have the Western Diversification Program which is now under a separate minister. These programs sometimes work at cross purposes. There is an overlap, an overlap of bureaucracy, an overlap of money that is going back and forth, and oftentimes at cross purposes
What we really need in this country is some real co-ordinating of programs. In fact, what we need is a minister who is responsible for rural affairs. Under that minister should be the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the Minister of Forestry, a minister of mining and northern development. That is what we should have, because when you stand in this House you cannot point to anyone who is responsible for rural affairs.
When this government, or any government, comes to its senses, that is the direction we will have to go. I see my time is starting to run out.
The third area where we have to make some changes is that federal governments in the past sat in Ottawa with bureaucrats or other politicians and developed programs and shoved them on to the regions. I know that when we were holding hearings on developing our rural policy and our rural paper for the New Democratic Party we heard time after time groups saying that they wanted to use program A or program B but they had to change the rules or adapt them in order to get the money, and after they got some money it never went to the full purpose and the full benefit it could have had they had more control over the money.
We need a government that facilitates and assists communities and grassroots organizations in developing their programs and helping with that development. The development of programs has to come not from Ottawa but from the regions. That is where the initiatives should come from. It is only logical but that is not what this government is doing.
In conclusion we need to ensure that the primary resource sector is primary to the future of rural Canada. We need to co-ordinate our programs. We should have a minister of rural affairs and a government that is a
facilitator and not a director of federal programs. In that way this government could save money, could cut the deficit and provide better jobs and a better lifestyle for all of rural Canada.
