Mr. Speaker, last autumn I put a question through the Chair to the Solicitor General regarding a matter involving the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.
I was seeking from him an assurance for Canadians that intelligence gathering and analysis had not been politicized. Politicization of that type of information can cause significant problems for democratic governments. There are many examples in modem history such as the case of J. Edgar Hoover in the United States who perhaps used information for purposes other than for that which it was originally intended in the field of security intelligence.
The background to my question involved two allegations that were publicly made. The first was that the names of intelligence sources were made known to the Solicitor General and were routinely disclosed. The second was that the political staff of the Solicitor General attended meetings of the target approval and review committee within CSIS.
On the first question the Solicitor General responded that in a small number of exceptional cases names were disclosed but in none of those cases was the person a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident. In that way he perhaps got a little lucky but that does not speak for other Solicitors General prior to this one. What he did not say but should have said, and he might if he had the chance, is that any reference in the Solicitor General's routine business to persons without using a code name should only occur on an exceptional need to know basis. I hope that is what is occurring because anything beyond that risks politicization.
The second question involved the allegation that political assistants of a previous solicitor general had attended meetings of the target approval and review committee. This was not fully addressed in the question.
A committee of this House reported in 1990 on CSIS and did not include that type of person at meetings of TARC. I hope that is the case. That is not to say that before 1988 such persons did not attend those meetings. I hope they did not. In any event we do not have a lot of information that they are now, and I believe they are not.
The point I want to make, and I make it on behalf of members on this side of the House for the benefit of the Solicitor General, is that disclosure of source names and attendance by political staff at meetings of TARC or any other committee within CSIS should not happen. It is a matter for continuing monitoring by the security and intelligence review committee that acts on behalf of this House and all Canadians in monitoring CSIS. The Solicitor General should always be in a position in this House to assure Canadians that the security intelligence gathering systems within CSIS are secure and have not been politicized as those public allegations suggested at that time.

Mr. Speaker, last June, the media did say that the names of CSIS's human sources were regularly passed on to politicians. More specifically, they said that the minister's instructions issued in 1986 described how CSIS's human sources should be treated and that the names of these informers should be disclosed to the Solicitor General of Canada.
Naturally, the director of the service keeps the minister informed on all important operational activities. The identity of human sources is a very sensitive issue and the promise of anonymity is a significant factor in obtaining their co-operation and trust. Their identity is always protected.
In this regard, Parliament gave the service an important responsibility which is found in section 18 of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act that reads as follows:
-no person shall disclose any information that the person obtained or to which the person had access in the course of the performance by that person of duties and functions under this Act or the participation by that person in the administration or enforcement of this Act and from which the identity of (a) any other person who is or was a confidential source of information or assistance to the Service-can be inferred.
February 2, 1993

There are departmental instructions dealing with human sources. Here, I would like to refer to On Course published by the government in February 1991.
Page 14 of this document contains the following statement: "Sources are to be managed so as to protect both the security of the service's operations and the personal safety of sources". Nevertheless, there is no requirement in these instructions to disclose the identity of a human source to the minister or another politician.
The identity of a human source will be revealed to the minister only if it is directly related to his responsibilities which is a very rare and exceptional occurrence.
In conclusion, the media's statements that the identity of human sources is regularly revealed to the Solicitor General are unfounded.

Mr. Speaker, my question was prompted by the death of a little six-year old girl in my riding, Dawn Shaw, who was raped and murdered by a person in the community.
The RCMP at that time were having some difficulty locating the perpetrator but a suspect has now been arrested. It was felt that the broad availability of DNA testing could have assisted in this matter. There is more precision in terms of identifying the perpetrator of the crime.
In fact rapists do not leave fingerprints but they do leave samples of tissues such as hair, semen and blood that can be analysed by forensic laboratories. Within a very narrow range those analyses can identify the perpetrator of the crime.
The people in the community were asking for the RCMP to have the right to administer DNA tests or take samples on the same basis as they would be able to obtain breath samples for driving under the influence of alcohol. This would result in a much more assured prosecution of the victims and it was therefore felt that there would be much more protection for women and children who are the prime victims of sexual assault by these people in the community.
I do not want to create the impression that all Canadians are targets of sexual assault. Ninety-two per cent of these assaults happen within the family and the perpetrator is a person known to the victim. The Ottawa Citizen at one time said you are mostly likely to be sexually assaulted by the person looking across from you at the breakfast table in the morning. Only 8 per cent of perpetrators are unknown to the victim.
I think the best way to deal with sexual assault within the family is to provide some kind of assistance to the family so that people who have a tendency to commit these crimes find out how they can stop. Many of them were victims of the previous generation.

February 2, 1993
Adjournment Debate
The other way to do it is to increase the certainty of detection and conviction and that is through using such screening processes as DNA typing. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Comox-Albemi has raised an important issue. As his question indicates at the moment there is no provision in the Criminal Code which permits a judge to authorize obtaining bodily substances, including samples suitable for DNA analysis, except in limited circumstances in relation to drunk driving charges.
In response to his specific concern, DNA testing could assist in positively identifying perpetrators of crimes, particularly in cases of sexual assault or homicide where identification is often the central issue.
I can inform hon. members that the Department of Justice is now conducting an in-depth study of the legal issues related to the collection and use of bodily substances for evidentiary purposes with a view to the development of proposals for amendments to the Criminal Code.
DNA profiling undoubtedly has the potential to facilitate the investigation and prosecution of criminal offences. However, the future of the role that DNA typing will play in our criminal justice system is dependent on a number of factors and there are various issues which must be examined within this context. The issues being explored include search and seizure, admissibility, evidence of population frequencies, data banks and the accreditation of laboratories.
Ultimately legislation would be needed to set out the manner and circumstances in which samples can be obtained from suspects so that the investigation of crimes is not frustrated and the suspects' rights to a
reasonable expectation of privacy and personal dignity as guaranteed by the charter are minimally interfered with.
The protection of society could well be enhanced by the enactment of legislative amendments to permit the seizure of samples of bodily substances for the purposes of DNA testing and the use of such forensic evidence in criminal prosecutions.

Mr. Speaker, tonight I would like to speak about the Gwa'Sala 'Nakwaxda'wx Indian people who live at Port Hardy at the Indian reserve at Tsulquate.
One particular group used to live at Blunden Harbour, the others at Smith Inlet. The Department of Indian Affairs for its sole convenience of cost of servicing asked them to move from their communities. They promised them housing, community infrastructure, education, economic development and health services. They were virtually forced out of the community by continued harassment and the promises that things would be better at the new location in Port Hardy.
They moved. Their houses were burned behind them when they asked to go back after none of the promises were kept.
When they hit Port Hardy they were amalgamated, two different groups. They did not know each other. They had no homes. They had no community. They had no infrastructure. They were not provided with education and school services and no health services. They were at the same time put into a community that had just received several thousand single men who were building a mine at the location. Those people wreaked absolute havoc on a completely disorganized community.
What were the results? Thirty years of indescribable hell brought on by almost complete alcoholism, complete total social destruction, despicable housing and desperate poverty and unemployment.
Is there anything that can happen? Thirty years later as this community is gradually rebuilding itself, two generations later, with the people who are just youngsters in the community, the government could visit the community at the highest level. The minister of Indian affairs should visit there.
February 2, 1993

Also, the senior leaders of government departments of employment, health, and Indian affairs should go and meet with the elders and the leaders of that community to discuss the health programs they developed for social rebuilding, employment programs and the responsibilities of Indian affairs.
Direct financial assistance is needed, compensation for the catastrophic impact that was forced on this community in the forced move, the forced amalgamation and the broken promises.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as stated by the minister in the House on June 12, 1992, he is certainly prepared to meet with the representatives of the Gwa'sala-Nakwaxda'xw on one of his future visits to British Columbia.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is familiar with the situation in this community on northern Vancouver Island. For some time now, departmental representatives at the district, regional and headquarters level have been making a joint effort to resolve as many problems in this community as they can, bearing in mind budgetary restrictions and general policy.
The specific claims of the Gwa'sala-Nakwaxda'xw were first submitted in 1988, re-submitted to the department in 1991, and then put on a priority list for research and analysis. On May 15, 1992, preliminary discussions took place between band representatives and the department's special claims office. It was agreed the Band should prepare a more thorough analysis of its claims before submitting them to the Department of Justice, to ensure the presentation would be as fair and detailed as possible.
Adjournment Debate
Meanwhile, the department is busy helping the community achieve its economic, cultural and educational objectives. The Band has just finished developing a comprehensive plan stating various options for promoting the community's expansion. With the 45.8 hectares added to Tkulquate Indian Reserve, No. 4, it will be possible to proceed with a new development that will include construction of 80 new homes, a school and a community hall.
Furthermore, the department plans to spend $1.6 million, spread over a certain period of time, in connection with the community's expansion. Funding totalling $200,000 will be released during 1992-93 and 1993-94, to help the Band build a community centre. Furthermore, $215,000 was spent in 1992-93 on improving sanitation in the community. Similarly, $15,000 will be spent on a preliminary feasibility study for the construction of a school; the plans should be finished by 1994-95, at a cost of $150,000, while construction is slated for 1995-96, at a cost of $1,250,000.
To help the Gwa'sala-Nakwaxda'xw find ways to resolve their financial problems, departmental representatives had a number of meetings with them. The band and the department have set up a joint committee that is now examining innovative proposals to meet the land requirements of the band.
Furthermore-and I speak on behalf of the minister- he says he is very interested in seeing the situation improve and is prepared to have discussions with the Gwa'sala-Nakwaxda'xw communities.
